1.intro: Square 1 in Leela is Genesis, janma in Sanskrit: the point of birth. Every player passes through it when the first six is thrown, before landing on square 6, Delusion. Genesis stands for the moment the wish to play binds you to karma, and the One, in Harish Johari's reading, begins to appear as many.
meaning: Harish Johari treats birth as entry into a karmic play. In his words, "the die is the karmic player, and the individual self a symbol." The token you place on the board is that symbol; the throws of the die are the karma that moves it. Square 1 marks the instant the symbol leaves its unborn rest and becomes a participant.

The Sanskrit janma simply means birth. Johari links it to desire: the wish to play is what ties a player to karma, and in entering the game you re-enact the old image of the One becoming many. Genesis is therefore neither good nor bad. It is the condition that makes every other square possible.

Genesis opens the first row, The Fundamentals of Being, which Johari connects with Muladhara, the root chakra at the base of the spine, and with the earth element. This row is about survival, possession and the basic passions, and it holds no arrows. Seen this way, square 1 teaches a simple point: before you ask what the game will show you, notice the desire that brought you to the board at all.

In play, Genesis is a square you pass rather than rest on. That makes it a good moment, before the first throw, to name the question you carry. Many players write it down while they wait on square 68 for their six, so that the path the symbol traces afterwards can be read against that intention.
1.board: Square 1 is not reached by an ordinary throw. Every player begins unborn on square 68, Cosmic Consciousness, and waits for a six. The entering six moves the symbol to square 1, Genesis, and on to square 6, Delusion, where the journey properly starts. No arrow and no snake leads into square 1, and it has no arrow or snake of its own. It sits in row 1, The Fundamentals of Being.
1.gita: The square is paired with Gita 2.27: birth is one turn of a long cycle, and all that is born will die and be born again. The Mahabharata episode of Karna's birth and abandonment shows how much of a life is shaped by a birth no one chose.
questions: What desire am I bringing into this game?
What would change if I saw this situation as one turn of a longer cycle?
Which circumstances of my starting point am I still arguing with?

2.intro: Square 2 in Leela is Illusion, maya in Sanskrit. It is the veiling power through which the One appears as many, and the spell of the game itself. Players reach it only by falling: the snake of Darkness on square 63 drops them here. It asks what in your situation might turn out to be an illusion.
meaning: For Harish Johari, maya is Maya Shakti, the power that veils unity and makes the world look divided and endlessly varied. It is also the fascination of play: the absorbing quality that makes a game feel real while it lasts. Maya is not a mistake to be blamed on the player. It is the medium in which the whole board exists.

Johari notes that two is the number of maya, because illusion begins the moment there is duality: self and other, mine and yours, like and dislike. Square 2 follows Genesis directly, as if to say that the first thing birth brings is a divided view.

Illusion sits in row 1, The Fundamentals of Being, linked with Muladhara, the root chakra, and the earth element. The link with the board's high end matters. The snake that lands here starts on square 63, Darkness, near the top of the board, so a player can travel almost all the way up and still be returned to the beginning of perception. The square teaches humility about certainty: what looks solid may be a pattern of the mind, and seeing it as such is already a step.

In practice, landing on Illusion is rarely dramatic in the moment; it shows itself afterwards, when a plan or a belief turns out to rest on less than it seemed. The square invites a slower look. Ask what you have been taking for granted, and what remains true once the colour and excitement fade.
2.board: Square 2 is reached by a snake, not by an ordinary throw. The snake of Darkness on square 63 carries a player from the seventh row straight down to Illusion. Since the entering six lands on square 6, a forward count never stops on 2. Square 2 has no arrow or snake of its own: from here the player simply moves on through row 1, The Fundamentals of Being, by the next throws.
2.gita: Gita 7.14 describes maya as woven from the gunas and hard to cross, yet seen through by whoever takes refuge in the Highest. The Maya Sabha, the hall of illusions in the Mahabharata, is its image: a palace where floors look like water and water looks like floor.
questions: What in my situation might turn out to be an illusion?
Which certainty of mine have I never tested against what is actually happening?
Where am I taking a difference on the surface for a real separation?

3.intro: Square 3 in Leela is Anger, krodh in Sanskrit. Harish Johari calls it the tail of the snake of egotism: a player on square 55, Egotism, falls straight here. Anger flares when the ego's attachments are touched, and the square asks a direct question: what in you is defending itself when you get angry?
meaning: Johari describes anger as what arises when the ego's identifications are hurt. Something you have taken to be yourself, a role, a possession, an opinion, an image, is threatened, and energy rushes to defend it. He calls this a downward projection of energy to the first chakra: a force that could rise instead drops to the level of survival.

The Sanskrit krodh (krodha) names this hot, sudden reaction. On the board it is bound to Egotism by a snake, and Johari's phrase "the tail of the snake of egotism" makes the link plain: anger is where pride lands when it is wounded. The higher the sense of self, the further it can fall.

Anger sits in row 1, The Fundamentals of Being, with Muladhara, the root chakra, and the earth element. It belongs among the basic passions, beside greed and delusion. The teaching is practical rather than moral. Anger is information: it points to what you are identified with. Seeing that clearly can turn an outburst into a moment of self-knowledge.

Working with this square does not mean suppressing anger. It means slowing down enough to see the moment the ego feels touched, before the heat takes over. Players often find that naming the hurt identification, quietly and honestly, takes much of the force out of the reaction and leaves the useful information behind.
3.board: Square 3 is reached in one of two ways. Most often a player arrives through the snake of Egotism, which carries a symbol from square 55 in the seventh row all the way down to 3. Otherwise it takes a throw of one from square 2, after a fall there; a normal count from the start never reaches it, because the game begins on square 6. Square 3 has no arrow or snake of its own; from here the player continues through row 1, The Fundamentals of Being.
3.gita: Gita 2.62 traces the chain from dwelling on an object to desire, from thwarted desire to anger, and then to confusion and the loss of reason. Bhima's vows in the dice hall show anger at its rawest: justified in its cause, terrible in what it sets in motion.
questions: What in me is defending itself when I get angry?
Which image of myself felt threatened just before the anger came?
Where did this anger start as a desire that was blocked?

4.intro: Square 4 in Leela is Greed, lobh in Sanskrit. Harish Johari describes it as inner emptiness mistaken for a lack of things: the more you take, the deeper the hole. Players arrive here when the snake of Jealousy on square 16 bites. The square asks a plain question: what emptiness are you trying to fill?
meaning: Johari defines greed as confusing inner unfulfilment with material need. A sense of something missing is real, but it is placed on the wrong object. Possessions, food, attention or success are gathered, and because they never touch the actual gap, acquiring more only deepens the emptiness.

The Sanskrit lobh (lobha) means craving or covetousness. Johari connects it with the snake that ends here: "Greed is the tail-end of the snake of jealousy." Jealousy, born of fantasy in the second row, is fear of losing what you have to a rival. When that fear takes hold, energy drops back to the first chakra and starts clutching.

Greed sits in row 1, The Fundamentals of Being, linked with Muladhara, the root chakra, and the earth element, the level of survival and possession. In that light greed is a survival reflex aimed at the wrong target. The square teaches discernment. Before reaching for more, ask what is actually lacking, and whether anything external could supply it.

In play, this square is a mirror for ordinary habits: the extra purchase, the second helping, the hours of scrolling, the hunger for one more success. None of these is condemned. The point is to notice the pattern, feel the gap underneath it, and ask what would actually meet that need instead of covering it.
4.board: Square 4 is reached through the snake of Jealousy: a player who lands on square 16, in the second row, slides down to Greed. Ordinary forward play starts on square 6, so a normal count does not stop here unless an earlier fall has placed the symbol on 2 or 3. Square 4 has no arrow or snake of its own. From here the player moves on through row 1, The Fundamentals of Being.
4.gita: Gita 14.17 names greed as a product of rajas that, with desire and anger, leads into darkness. The game of dice in the Mahabharata shows where the restless wish for more can lead, as a kingdom, brothers and finally Draupadi are staked.
questions: What emptiness am I trying to fill?
What would be enough, if I said it in plain numbers or plain words?
Which fear of losing something is making me hold on tighter?

5.intro: Square 5 in Leela is the Physical plane, bhu-loka in Sanskrit: earth, body and your store of energy. It is the first of the seven lokas that run up the centre of Harish Johari's board, the ground the whole path stands on. The square asks a grounding question: how are your body and your footing right now?
meaning: Johari calls the physical plane the storehouse of energy and the seat of kundalini, the coiled potential that yoga traditions place at the base of the spine. Everything a player later experiences, from fantasy to devotion, draws on the energy held at this level. It is the foundation, not something to escape.

Bhu-loka means the earth world. It is the first of the seven lokas, or planes, that form the central column of the board: 5, 14, 23, 32, 41, 50 and 59, rising to 68, Cosmic Consciousness. Johari calls these lokas "the spine of the game board", so square 5 is the lowest vertebra of that spine.

The square sits in the middle of row 1, The Fundamentals of Being, linked with Muladhara, the root chakra, and the earth element. Johari observes that no arrows lead out of this row, while "seven snakes lead here from other planes". The first level is where most falls end. The physical plane teaches respect for the body and for basic stability: rest, food, money, health and place are the soil in which inner work grows.

For a player, square 5 is a reminder to check the basics before anything else. A tired body, unstable finances or an unsettled home colour every question you bring to the game. Johari's picture of energy stored at the base suggests a simple practice: restore what you have spent, so there is something to raise.
5.board: No arrow and no snake leads to square 5, and it has none of its own. Because the entering six places the symbol on square 6, a player reaches the Physical plane only after a fall to square 2, 3 or 4, followed by an ordinary throw that counts forward onto 5. From here play continues through row 1, The Fundamentals of Being, toward the second row.
5.gita: Gita 7.4 names earth as the first element of Krishna's lower nature, firm ground to lean on but only the start. In the episode of the burden of Earth, the goddess Earth asks for help under the weight she carries, and the gods descend to answer.
questions: How are my body and my footing right now?
Where am I spending energy faster than I am restoring it?
What practical ground needs attention before I can think about anything higher?

6.intro: Square 6 in Leela is Delusion, moha in Sanskrit: clinging to what is visible as the only reality. Every journey begins here, because the first six carries the newborn symbol from Genesis to square 6. Players also return to it through the snake of Irreligiosity on square 29. The square asks what you believe without ever checking.
meaning: Harish Johari defines moha as attachment to the phenomenal world as the only reality. What can be seen, touched and counted is taken to be all there is, and the mind closes around that picture. Johari calls delusion the product of irreligiosity: when one loses connection with any larger order, the visible world becomes the whole world.

Every player passes through this state on entry. That is a striking design choice: the game does not begin in innocence but in delusion, as if to say that every life starts inside a limited view. Johari adds that a closed worldview keeps bringing the player back, so Delusion is both a starting point and a frequent return.

Moha means bewilderment or infatuation, the fog that comes from attachment. The square sits in row 1, The Fundamentals of Being, with Muladhara, the root chakra, and the earth element. Its teaching is gentle. Delusion is the common ground of all players, not a personal failing. What matters is noticing it: questioning a belief you have never examined is how the climb begins.

Practically, the square invites a modest experiment. Take one belief that feels obviously true, about yourself, another person or the way the world works, and look for what it leaves out. Delusion loosens not through argument but through attention, and the board places this work right at the start because everything later depends on it.
6.board: Square 6 is where play truly starts. Every player waits on square 68 until a six is thrown; the six counts from square 1, Genesis, and lands the symbol on 6, Delusion. Later, the snake of Irreligiosity on square 29, in the fourth row, brings players back here. Square 6 has no arrow or snake of its own, so from here the player moves forward through row 1, The Fundamentals of Being.
6.gita: Gita 7.27 says all beings are born into delusion, bred by the pairs of like and dislike. Arjuna's despair on the battlefield is the great example: overwhelmed at the start of the Gita, he can say by its end that his delusion is gone.
questions: What do I believe without ever checking?
Which like or dislike is shaping how I see this situation?
What would I notice if I assumed my current view was incomplete?

7.intro: Square 7 in Leela is Conceit, mada in Sanskrit: self-intoxication, false pride, castles in the air. Players arrive here when the snake of Bad company on square 24 drops them down from the third row. The square asks a sharp, useful question: where do you want to seem rather than be?
meaning: Harish Johari describes mada as self-intoxication. The word carries the sense of drunkenness, and conceit works like a drink: it warms, inflates and blurs judgement. Johari's image of "castles in the air" captures it well, grand structures of self-image with nothing underneath to hold them up.

On the board, conceit is the landing place of the snake of bad company. Johari writes that "bad company... is the snake that leads the player to conceit." The people and influences around you shape how you see yourself. Company that flatters, competes or feeds illusions lets pride grow without any check from reality.

Conceit sits in row 1, The Fundamentals of Being, with Muladhara, the root chakra, and the earth element. Johari also says conceit gives birth to avarice on square 8, so pride and grasping stand side by side. The teaching is about honesty. Conceit is not confidence; it is a gap between the image and the person. Noticing where you perform rather than live is the first step toward closing that gap.

In play, conceit often hides behind good qualities: competence that wants applause, generosity that needs to be seen, spirituality that keeps score. The square does not ask you to shrink. It asks you to separate the work from the show, and to notice which people around you help you do that and which make it harder.
7.board: Square 7 is reached mainly through the snake of Bad company: a player who lands on square 24, in the third row, falls back to Conceit. It can also be reached by an ordinary throw from squares 2 to 6, for example a throw of one from Delusion at the very start of play. Square 7 has no arrow or snake of its own. From here the player keeps moving forward through row 1, The Fundamentals of Being.
7.gita: Gita 16.4 names hypocrisy, arrogance and conceit as the first marks of the demonic nature. The fall of Nahusha, a king who rose to rule heaven and was cast down by his own arrogance, shows how quickly self-intoxication can reverse a climb.
questions: Where do I want to seem rather than be?
Whose company makes my self-image grow faster than my actual work?
Which castle in the air am I defending right now?

8.intro: Square 8 in Leela is Avarice, matsar or matsarya in Sanskrit: greed joined with envy, a resentment of what others have. It is the tail of the board's first snake, Envy on square 12. Harish Johari says avarice is born of conceit. The square asks an uncomfortable but freeing question: whose good fortune stings you, and why?
meaning: Johari describes avarice as greed coupled with envy. Greed alone wants more; avarice also minds that others have it. It looks sideways at someone else's possessions, success or happiness and feels spite. In this sense avarice is less about getting and more about comparing.

The Sanskrit matsar, or matsarya, carries this mix of jealousy and meanness. Johari places its birth in conceit, the square just before it: once you are inflated by false pride, the success of others feels like an insult. He also writes that "avarice is linked with the snake of envy", and on the board the first snake of the game, from square 12, ends here.

Avarice sits in row 1, The Fundamentals of Being, with Muladhara, the root chakra, and the earth element. It completes a cluster of first-row passions: anger, greed, delusion, conceit and avarice. The teaching is practical. Spite toward another person's fortune points straight at a desire of your own. Naming that desire honestly takes the sting out of comparison.

In a reading of your own game, a stop on Avarice is a chance to look at comparison directly. Whose life do you measure yours against? Envy often goes quiet once the wish behind it is named and taken seriously, because energy spent resenting another person can then be turned toward your own path.
8.board: Square 8 is reached through the snake of Envy, the first snake of the game: a player who lands on square 12, in the second row, falls back to Avarice. It can also be reached by an ordinary throw from squares 2 to 7. Square 8 has no arrow or snake of its own. From here the player continues forward through row 1, The Fundamentals of Being.
8.gita: Gita 4.22 describes the sage as content with what comes unasked and free of envy. The story of Drona and Drupada, childhood friends divided when one became a king and refused to share, shows how a grudge over what another holds can shape a whole life.
questions: Whose good fortune stings me, and why?
What do I actually want that this comparison is pointing to?
Where could I share more freely what I am holding tightly?

9.intro: Square 9 in Leela is the Sensual plane, kama-loka in Sanskrit: the plane of desires of every kind. Harish Johari calls it the first stage of evolution and the ladder to purification in the next row. Players reach it by gradual passage or through the snake of Ignorance on square 44. It asks which desire is leading you right now.
meaning: Johari treats kama, desire, as the driving force of the first stage of evolution. Without desire nothing moves: the player would never leave the base of the board. Square 9 is therefore not a trap but a threshold, the last square of row 1 and the step that leads up to row 2 and Purification on square 10.

Kama-loka means the world or plane of desire. In Johari's reading it holds desire in all its forms, from bodily appetites to ambition and longing. The question is not whether to desire but which desires lead somewhere and which simply repeat. Desire that is noticed and refined becomes the ladder he describes.

The Sensual plane closes row 1, The Fundamentals of Being, with Muladhara, the root chakra, and the earth element. Johari says it can be reached "through the mouth of the snake of ignorance", from square 44, or by gradual passage through the row. That double approach teaches something: desire can be a step forward after patient work, or a fall back when knowledge is forgotten.

In play, the Sensual plane is a place to look at desire without shame and without indulgence. The square stands at the very edge of the first row, so whatever desire you name here is also the one you carry upward. Seeing it clearly is how the next square, Purification, becomes possible.
9.board: Square 9 is reached in two ways. Players coming up through row 1 arrive by an ordinary throw from squares 3 to 8. Players high on the board can fall here through the snake of Ignorance, which carries a symbol from square 44, in the fifth row, down to 9. Square 9 has no arrow or snake of its own; it is the last square of row 1, and the next step leads to Purification on square 10.
9.gita: Gita 3.39 says desire hides knowledge as smoke hides fire, yet desire in line with dharma is also divine. King Yayati, who traded years of youth to go on enjoying, learned at length that desire is not quenched by feeding it.
questions: Which desire is leading me right now?
Which of my desires would still feel right a year from now?
What does this desire ask me to refine rather than give up?

10.intro: Square 10 in Leela is Purification, shuddhi in Sanskrit, and it holds the first arrow of the game. Changing your senses, actions and daily habits lifts you straight from square 10 to square 23, the Celestial plane. It opens row 2, The Realm of Fantasy. The square asks which habit you are ready to let go of.
meaning: Harish Johari writes that "purification is the first arrow of the game." In his account, the player raises his vibration by reforming the senses, the organs of action and daily habits, and this lifts him "immediately to the celestial plane." Purification here is concrete: what you eat, watch, say and repeat each day.

The Sanskrit shuddhi means cleansing or purity. It does not mean rejecting the body or the world. It means removing what clouds perception, so that energy collected on the sensual plane can rise instead of circling. It is fitting that square 10 follows the Sensual plane directly: desire, once refined, becomes the lift.

Purification opens row 2, The Realm of Fantasy, linked with Svadhisthana, the second chakra, and the water element. Water is the classic image of cleansing. The arrow from 10 to 23 jumps a whole row and lands in the third, The Theater of Karma. The teaching is hopeful and practical: small, steady changes in habit can move a person further than effort spent only in thought.

In reflective play the arrow is a reminder that change is often simpler than it looks. A single habit adjusted with care, kept over time, can shift how the senses work and how energy moves. Players landing here often take it as encouragement to choose one concrete practice rather than many vague intentions.
10.board: Square 10 is reached by an ordinary throw from squares 4 to 9, as the player leaves the first row. No arrow or snake leads into it. Landing here triggers the first arrow of the game: the symbol rises at once from square 10 to square 23, the Celestial plane, in row 3. Square 10 itself opens row 2, The Realm of Fantasy.
10.gita: Gita 5.11 describes acting with body, mind and senses, free of attachment, for self-purification. Arjuna's penance and his meeting with the Kirata, Shiva in the guise of a hunter, show discipline humbled and refined before a higher gift is given.
questions: Which habit am I ready to let go of?
What do I take in each day, through eyes, ears or mouth, that leaves me heavier?
Which small daily practice would make the biggest difference if I kept it?

11.intro: Square 11 in Leela is Entertainment, named after the gandharvas, the celestial musicians of Indian tradition. It stands for lightness, play and art, and Harish Johari calls entertainment "the essence of the spirit." It is a plain square in row 2, with no arrow or snake. It asks where your question is missing some lightness.
meaning: After the heavy passions of the first row, square 11 brings relief. Johari places the gandharvas here: beings of music, rhythm and beauty who entertain the gods. Their presence on the board says that joy is not a distraction from inner work but part of it. He calls entertainment "the essence of the spirit".

The gandharvas belong to the mythology of the Vedas and epics, singers and players of the heavenly courts. Naming a square after them gives play a dignity of its own. Lightness, humour and art loosen the grip of the ego and help a person hold serious matters without being crushed by them.

Entertainment sits in row 2, The Realm of Fantasy, linked with Svadhisthana, the second chakra, and the water element. This is the row where imagination and the senses awaken, and square 11 is its first easy breath. The teaching is balanced. Play renews energy and opens creativity, yet the next squares, Envy and Nullity, show that a life of entertainment alone can turn hollow.

For a player, square 11 can be the most useful corrective on the board. Many people bring heavy questions to Leela and treat every square with grave seriousness. Entertainment reminds you that the whole board is itself a play, lila, and that a lighter touch often lets you see more, not less.
11.board: Square 11 is a plain square: no arrow or snake leads to it, and it has none of its own. A player reaches it by an ordinary throw from squares 5 to 9, since square 10 is an arrow base that carries anyone landing there up to 23. From square 11 play continues through row 2, The Realm of Fantasy, with Envy on square 12 just ahead.
11.gita: In Gita 10.26 Krishna says that among the gandharvas he is Chitraratha, a sign that music and play can also lead to the Highest. In the Mahabharata, Arjuna learns music and dance from the gandharva Chitrasena during his stay in heaven.
questions: Where is my question missing some lightness?
When did I last play or make something only for the joy of it?
Could I hold this problem more lightly without taking it less seriously?

12.intro: Square 12 in Leela is Envy, eirsha in Sanskrit, and it holds the first snake of the game. A player who lands here falls from square 12 down to square 8, Avarice. Harish Johari says envy is felt when one has reached a higher plane by chance and feels unworthy. It asks what you envy and what that reveals about your own desire.
meaning: Johari writes: "Envy is the first snake of the game. Its bite brings the player down from the second chakra to avarice." He gives a subtle cause. Envy arises when a player has reached a higher plane through karmic chance, without yet feeling equal to it, and so looks at others with a sense of being less.

The Sanskrit eirsha (irshya) means envy or jealous resentment. Unlike greed, which wants things, envy looks at people: their gifts, success, ease. Behind it, Johari suggests, lies a feeling of unworthiness. That is why envy drops the player back into avarice, greed mixed with spite, in the first row.

Envy sits in row 2, The Realm of Fantasy, linked with Svadhisthana, the second chakra, and the water element. Here imagination wakes, and with it the habit of comparing your inner life to the imagined lives of others. The teaching is clear and kind: envy is a pointer. It shows a desire you have not yet owned, and a worth you have not yet accepted in yourself.

In play, landing on Envy can feel unfair, since it follows so soon after the lightness of Entertainment. Yet the fall is short, from the second row to the first, and the way back up is open. The square asks you to admit the comparison, own the desire inside it, and continue from Avarice with clearer eyes.
12.board: Square 12 is reached by an ordinary throw from squares 6 to 9 or from square 11; no arrow or snake leads into it. Landing here triggers the first snake of the game: the symbol falls from square 12, in row 2, The Realm of Fantasy, back to square 8, Avarice, in row 1. The next throw is made from square 8.
12.gita: Gita 3.32 warns that whoever carps and envies loses the way. Duryodhana in the Maya Sabha, burning at the splendour of his cousins' hall and humiliated by its illusions, shows envy turning into the resentment that leads toward war.
questions: What do I envy, and what does it reveal about my own desire?
Where do I feel I have not earned the place I am in?
What would change if I treated another person's success as information rather than a threat?

13.intro: Square 13 in Leela is Nullity, antariksha in Sanskrit: the empty space between earth and heaven. It names the hollow, restless feeling that follows energy spent without purpose. It sits in the second row, the Realm of Fantasy, and it is also where the snake of Negative intellect (61) drops a player. Johari treats it as a passing state.
meaning: Harish Johari describes Nullity as the space between, a gap where meaning seems to drain away. It comes after energy has been scattered: plans fall flat, effort feels pointless, and the mind cannot settle. Johari is clear that this is transient. Nothing is fixed here; the feeling is real, but it is not a verdict.

The Sanskrit antariksha means the intermediate region, the atmosphere that hangs between the earth below and the heavens above. The image fits the state: you are no longer grounded in simple needs, yet you have not found a higher footing either. You hang in the air, and that suspension is what feels like emptiness.

Nullity belongs to the second row, the Realm of Fantasy, governed by the Svadhisthana chakra and the element of water. In this row the senses and the imagination wake up, and imagination can just as easily dissolve into vagueness. Square 13 teaches the player to notice where strength is leaking away. It also teaches patience: the empty pause is a place to stand still, take stock and let the next movement come, rather than a place to stay. In Johari's sequence, the squares that follow offer mercy and charity, so the gap is always close to a way forward.
13.board: Square 13 is a plain square in row 2, the Realm of Fantasy: it has no arrow and no snake of its own. A player reaches it by an ordinary throw from earlier squares, or falls here from far above, because the snake of Negative intellect at square 61 lands on 13. From here play simply continues, and two arrows lie close ahead: Mercy at 17 and Charity at 20.
13.gita: In Gita 6.38 Arjuna fears vanishing like a torn cloud, with no footing here or beyond, and Krishna answers that whoever does good is never lost; Nullity is that pause, not an ending. The Mahabharata mirrors it in Yudhishthira's despair after the war.
questions: Where am I losing meaning and strength?
What did I recently pour energy into that left me feeling empty?
What small, honest step would give me footing again?

14.intro: Square 14 in Leela is the Astral plane, bhuvar-loka in Sanskrit: the world of dreams, imagination and possibility. It is the central square of the second row, the Realm of Fantasy, and the second of the lokas that form the spine of the board. Its gift is a widening inner world; its risk is drifting away into fantasy.
meaning: Johari presents the Astral plane as the second loka, linked to the element of water. After the first row, where life is about survival, security and the body, the player discovers a whole inner landscape: dreams, images, plans and possibilities that the physical world alone could never offer. The world becomes larger than what the eyes can see.

Bhuvar-loka is the second of the seven worlds of Indian cosmology, the realm that lies just above bhu-loka, the earth. On the Leela board the lokas run up the central column like vertebrae: 5, 14, 23, 32, 41, 50, 59 and finally 68. Square 14 is the second step on that spine, at the heart of the Svadhisthana chakra.

The lesson of square 14 is double. Imagination is a real power: it lets you picture another life, create, and sense more than what is in front of you. Yet the same fluid quality can carry you off, so that you live in what might be rather than in what is. Johari names this risk plainly: being swept away by fantasy. A player on the Astral plane is invited to enjoy the richness of the inner world while staying awake to the difference between a vision and a step taken.
14.board: Square 14 is a plain square at the centre of row 2, the Realm of Fantasy. No arrow or snake begins or ends here, so a player only arrives by an ordinary throw from the squares below. Nothing moves you on: you stay on the Astral plane until the next throw. Ahead in the same row lie the Plane of fantasy (15), the snake of Jealousy (16) and the arrow of Mercy (17).
14.gita: Gita 18.35 describes tamasic resolve as the kind that clings to sleep, fear and grief; the dream world beckons, but the sage stays awake where others sleep. The Mahabharata episode of the dead rising from the Ganga for one night shows how powerful, and how brief, such visions are.
questions: What am I dreaming while awake?
Which of my plans lives only in my head?
What vision is worth turning into one concrete action this week?

15.intro: Square 15 in Leela is the Plane of fantasy, naga-loka in Sanskrit. It stands for free, unrestrained imagination, the source from which art is born. Because naga means snake, Johari calls it the snake plane, and the very next square is the snake of Jealousy. Square 15 celebrates creative freedom and shows how close it sits to its shadow.
meaning: For Johari, the Plane of fantasy is imagination without limits. Here the mind is free to invent, to play with images and to create worlds. This is the fertile ground of painting, music, poetry and every kind of creative work. After the Astral plane opens the inner world, square 15 shows what imagination can do when it is let loose. Nothing here is yet wrong; imagination is simply free.

The Sanskrit name naga-loka means the world of the nagas, the serpent beings of Indian myth who live in the waters and the underworld and guard hidden treasures. On a board of snakes and arrows the name is a deliberate signal: this is the snake plane. Unbounded fantasy carries a hidden risk, and the risk is waiting one step away.

The square belongs to the second row, the Realm of Fantasy, ruled by the Svadhisthana chakra and the element of water. Water takes any shape, and so does imagination. The same power that creates a song can also imagine a rival, a betrayal, a loss that has not happened. That is the path from 15 to 16. The teaching here is to keep fantasy as a creative force while watching the moment it starts producing fear and suspicion.
15.board: Square 15 is a plain square in row 2, the Realm of Fantasy. No arrow or snake leads here, so a player arrives by a normal throw, and nothing moves you on once you land. The danger lies directly ahead: square 16, Jealousy, is a snake down to 4 Greed. One square beyond it, 17 Mercy is an arrow up to 69, the Absolute plane.
15.gita: Gita 2.67 warns that a mind chasing the wandering senses carries reason off as the wind drives a boat on the water; fantasy is fine as long as you hold the rudder. The Mahabharata tells of Ulupi taking Arjuna down to the land of the Nagas, a journey into the very world this square is named after.
questions: Which of my fantasies wants to become real?
Where does my imagination create, and where does it start to frighten me?
What would I make if I trusted my imagination fully?

16.intro: Square 16 in Leela is Jealousy, dwesh in Sanskrit, and it is a snake. Landing here sends the player down to square 4, Greed, in the first row. Johari describes jealousy as suspicion and fear of a rival, born of fantasy that has been overindulged. The bite pulls energy back from the second chakra to the first.
meaning: Johari places Jealousy right after the Plane of fantasy for a reason. Imagination that runs unchecked begins to invent threats: someone who could take your place, your partner, your recognition. Jealousy is that fear of a rival, and it feeds on images more than facts. The suspicion grows in the mind long before anything happens outside.

The Sanskrit dwesh (dvesha) means aversion or hostility, the pushing away of what we dislike. It is the twin of raga, attraction. Together they are the pair that Indian philosophy sees behind most suffering. Jealousy is aversion turned toward a person who seems to threaten what we hold, and it is never far from wanting to hold more.

That is why the snake ends at Greed. In Johari's reading, the jealous player's energy is drawn back to the first chakra, Muladhara, where the urge to grasp and accumulate takes over. Square 16 sits in the second row, the Realm of Fantasy, under the Svadhisthana chakra, and it shows how a fall begins: not from a deed but from an imagined loss. The teaching is to recognise the fear early and see it for what it is, a story the mind is telling.
16.board: Square 16 is the head of a snake in row 2, the Realm of Fantasy. A player arrives by an ordinary throw, often just after the Plane of fantasy (15); no arrow or snake from elsewhere ends here. Landing on 16 sends you straight down to square 4, Greed, in row 1. It is the second snake of the game, after Envy at 12. One square further on, 17 Mercy would have been an arrow up to 69.
16.gita: Gita 3.34 teaches that attraction and aversion sit in every sense, lying in wait for the seeker, and that the true renunciate neither hates nor craves; jealousy is that aversion catching you. The Mahabharata's house of lac, ordered by Duryodhana to burn the Pandavas he envied, shows where such fear of a rival can lead.
questions: What am I afraid of losing?
Is the rival I fear real, or did my imagination build them?
What would I hold more lightly if I trusted what I already have?

17.intro: Square 17 in Leela is Mercy, daya in Sanskrit, and it holds one of the longest arrows on the board. Landing here lifts the player from the second row straight to square 69, the Absolute plane. Johari explains that compassion and forgiveness strong enough carry a person from the second chakra to the eighth level, though past karma is not yet spent.
meaning: Johari describes Mercy as compassion and the power to forgive, so strong that it changes the player's whole level at once. After the fears and envies of the second row, square 17 shows the opposite movement: instead of contracting around a loss, the heart opens and lets go of the grievance. That release is enough, in the logic of the board, to carry the player past every chakra.

The Sanskrit daya means compassion, kindness, the wish to relieve another's suffering. In Indian ethics it is counted among the noblest qualities. Daya does not mean weakness or approving harm. It means seeing the other clearly and still choosing not to strike back.

Yet Johari adds a sober note. The arrow of Mercy lands on 69, the Absolute plane in the eighth row, not on 68, Cosmic consciousness, the goal. The player has leapt beyond the chakras while their karma remains, so the game is not finished. From the top row the only way down is the snake of Inertia (tamoguna) at 72, which returns the player to 51, Earth. Square 17 teaches that forgiveness is immensely powerful, and that a sudden leap does not replace the slow work still to be done.
17.board: Square 17 is the foot of an arrow in row 2, the Realm of Fantasy, just after the snake of Jealousy at 16. A player reaches it by an ordinary throw; no other arrow or snake leads here. Landing on 17 lifts you directly to square 69, the Absolute plane, in row 8, beyond the chakras. Play then continues in the top row, where square 72, Inertia (tamoguna), is a snake back down to 51 Earth.
17.gita: Gita 16.2 counts compassion for all beings among the divine qualities, while warning of a false pity that paralyses; true mercy is clear and strong. In the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira refuses to enter heaven without the dog that followed him, compassion that will not abandon even the humblest companion.
questions: Whom could I forgive today?
Is there a grudge I keep because it protects me?
How would I treat myself if I showed myself the same mercy?

18.intro: Square 18 in Leela is the Plane of joy, harsha-loka in Sanskrit. It closes the second row, the Realm of Fantasy, and names the contentment of having moved past envy, nullity and jealousy. Johari calls this joy eternal yet brief: it is fully real in the moment, and then karma carries the player into the third row.
meaning: Johari describes square 18 as the satisfaction that comes after the trials of the second row. The player has passed Envy at 12, Nullity at 13 and Jealousy at 16 without being pulled down, and a quiet gladness follows. It is not the excitement of winning something, but the lightness of no longer being gripped by comparison and fear.

The Sanskrit harsha means joy, delight, the thrill of gladness, and loka means world or plane. Harsha-loka is the world of joy. The paradox Johari names is that this joy is eternal and momentary at once. Joy itself never runs out as a possibility; any single experience of it passes quickly.

As the last square of the row ruled by the Svadhisthana chakra and the element of water, the Plane of joy marks the end of a stage. In Johari's life cycles the second row matches the years from seven to fourteen, the age of fantasy, and joy here feels like the end of childhood play. Then karma begins: the next square, 19, opens the Theater of Karma. Square 18 teaches the player to receive joy fully without trying to hold it, so that its passing does not become a new loss.
18.board: Square 18 is a plain square at the end of row 2, the Realm of Fantasy. No arrow or snake begins or ends here, so a player arrives only by an ordinary throw, having moved beyond Envy (12) and Jealousy (16). Nothing moves you on. Your next throw takes you into row 3, the Theater of Karma, which begins at square 19, the Plane of action.
18.gita: Gita 5.20 describes the sage who neither exults at the pleasant nor grieves at the unpleasant; real, sattvic joy is quiet and grows from within, not from luck. The Mahabharata's svayamvara where Arjuna wins Draupadi is a moment of great joy that also sets the coming story in motion.
questions: What am I truly glad about right now?
What have I recently let go of that made me lighter?
Can I enjoy this moment without needing it to last?

19.intro: Square 19 in Leela is the Plane of action, karma-loka in Sanskrit. It opens the third row, the Theater of Karma, and the Manipura chakra. Here the desire for fulfilment starts to seek identity, power and recognition, and with it comes the first real understanding of cause and effect: every action has consequences, and the player begins to see them.
meaning: Johari places the Plane of action at the start of the third chakra. In the second row the player lived largely in imagination; now desire turns outward and wants results. The player looks for a place in the world, for strength, status and the respect of others. This is the energy that builds careers, takes on challenges and wants to matter.

The Sanskrit karma means action, and also the chain of consequences that action sets in motion. Karma-loka is the world where that chain becomes visible. On square 19 the player begins to understand that what happens to them is not random: today's situation has roots in yesterday's choices, and today's choices are planting tomorrow. Seeing this is not a burden but a kind of freedom, because what was set in motion can also be redirected.

The third row is ruled by Manipura, the navel chakra, and the element of fire. Fire gives drive, digestion and will, and it can also burn. In Johari's life cycles this row matches the years from fourteen to twenty one, the age of identity and power. Square 19 teaches responsibility without guilt: seeing your actions and their effects clearly is the ground on which charity, atonement and dharma, the next squares, can grow.
19.board: Square 19 is a plain square at the start of row 3, the Theater of Karma. No arrow or snake leads here, so a player arrives by an ordinary throw from the second row. Nothing moves you on. Ahead lies the most decisive row for upward movement: Charity (20) rises to 32, Dharma (22) to 60 and Selfless service (27) to 41, while Bad company (24) falls to 7.
19.gita: Gita 3.5 states that no embodied being can stay inactive even for a moment, because the gunas keep moving it; the question is not whether to act, but how. The Mahabharata's curse of Mandavya, where a sage is punished for a cruelty done as a child, shows how long the thread of cause and effect can run.
questions: Which consequences of my actions am I living with today?
Where am I seeking recognition, and what would happen if I stopped?
What am I planting now that I will meet later?

20.intro: Square 20 in Leela is Charity, daan in Sanskrit, and it is an arrow. Landing here lifts the player from the third row to square 32, the Plane of balance, in the heart row. Johari describes charity as giving without seeking any personal benefit. That kind of giving moves the player beyond the search for power into the steadiness of the heart.
meaning: Johari places Charity just after the Plane of action, where the player has begun to seek recognition and power. Square 20 shows the turn: instead of gathering, the player gives. The point is not the size of the gift but the absence of calculation. Giving to be seen, to be thanked or to gain influence stays inside the third chakra; giving freely leaves it behind.

The Sanskrit daan (dana) means giving, the gift, generosity. In Indian traditions it is one of the core practices of ethical life, honoured in every school. Dana can be material, but it also includes time, attention, knowledge and protection. What makes it dana is the spirit in which it is offered. A small gift given freely weighs more on this board than a large one given with conditions.

This is why the arrow lands on 32, the Plane of balance, at the centre of the fourth row and the Anahata, or heart, chakra. Genuine generosity loosens the grip of the lower desires: when you can give without needing a return, you are no longer ruled by lack. Johari also notes that charity, together with mercy, can rescue a player who has fallen to Nullity. Square 20 teaches that open hands bring balance.
20.board: Square 20 is the foot of an arrow in row 3, the Theater of Karma. A player reaches it by an ordinary throw from the squares just before it; one who has fallen to square 13, Nullity, is only a few squares away. No other arrow or snake ends here. Landing on 20 lifts you to square 32, the Plane of balance, the central square of row 4 and the Anahata chakra.
20.gita: Gita 17.20 describes sattvic giving as a gift made simply because it is right, to one who cannot repay, at the right time and place; given without expecting a return, it frees the giver. Karna, who gives away his protective armour and earrings to the one who asks, embodies this in the Mahabharata.
questions: What can I give without expecting anything back?
When I give, what am I secretly hoping to receive?
What do I have plenty of that someone near me lacks?

21.intro: Square 21 in Leela is Atonement, saman paap in Sanskrit. It stands for the moment a player sees the harm done while chasing lower needs and sincerely wants to make amends. Johari describes this as restoring the right vibration. It sits in the third row, the Theater of Karma, and leads directly into square 22, the Plane of dharma.
meaning: After the Plane of action and the arrow of Charity, square 21 turns the player's attention backward. In seeking power and recognition, people get hurt along the way: promises are broken, others are used, the self is betrayed. Johari describes Atonement as becoming aware of that harm and wanting to put it right. The emphasis is on awareness and repair, not on guilt. Seeing clearly is always the first step.

The Sanskrit saman paap can be read as the settling or neutralising of paap, wrongdoing. Paap is the weight of actions that went against what was right. Atonement does not erase the past; it changes how the player carries it. By naming the harm and making amends where possible, the distorted energy of those actions is brought back into balance.

The square belongs to the third row, the Theater of Karma, under the Manipura chakra and the element of fire. Fire purifies, and atonement is a kind of inner fire that burns away the residue of past mistakes. Johari notes that making amends leads into dharma, the next square: once you have repaired what you broke, you are ready to act in harmony with the order of things. Square 21 teaches that mistakes are not final.
21.board: Square 21 is a plain square in row 3, the Theater of Karma. No arrow or snake begins or ends here, so a player arrives by an ordinary throw, often just after Charity at 20. Nothing moves you on. Directly ahead is square 22, the Plane of dharma, whose arrow rises to 60, Positive intellect. Further along the row, square 24, Bad company, is a snake down to 7.
21.gita: Gita 4.36 teaches that past mistakes are not final: even the worst wrongdoer crosses the sea of evil in the boat of knowledge. In the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira bows before Gandhari, the mother who lost all her sons in the war, and faces her grief instead of turning away.
questions: What do I want to put right?
Whom have I hurt while chasing what I wanted?
What would a sincere first step toward repair look like?

22.intro: Square 22 in Leela is the Plane of dharma, dharma-loka in Sanskrit, and it holds one of the strongest arrows in the game. Landing here lifts the player from the third row to square 60, Positive intellect, in the seventh row. Johari defines dharma as conscious action in harmony with the cosmic order, and he calls the arrows of the board dharmas, virtues.
meaning: For Johari, dharma is the axis of the whole game. He describes it as conscious action in accord with the law that holds the universe together, and he gives ten signposts of it as guides for living. He also states the board's central idea: the arrows are dharmas, virtues, and the snakes are adharmas, vices. Square 22 is the plane where that principle is met directly.

The Sanskrit dharma comes from a root meaning to hold or to support. Dharma is what holds a life upright: duty, right conduct, the inner law of one's own nature. Dharma-loka is the world in which action is aligned with that law. It follows Atonement on the board: once the harm of the past is repaired, the player can act rightly.

The arrow is long because dharma touches every level. From the Manipura chakra and the fire of the third row, the player is lifted to 60, Positive intellect, in the Sahasrara row. Johari explains that positive intellect is reached by following the path of dharma, which is exactly where this arrow ends. Square 22 teaches that clear thinking grows from living rightly, and that knowing one's duty and acting on it is itself an ascent.
22.board: Square 22 is the foot of an arrow in row 3, the Theater of Karma, right after Atonement at 21. A player reaches it by an ordinary throw; no other arrow or snake ends here. Landing on 22 lifts you to square 60, Positive intellect, in row 7, the Plane of Reality, under the Sahasrara chakra. It is one of the longest climbs on the board, from row 3 to row 7.
22.gita: Gita 4.7 says that when dharma weakens, the Divine comes to restore it; your path now is to understand what duty asks of you and stand on its side. In the Mahabharata, Vidura, wise counsellor and dharma embodied, keeps speaking for what is right in a court that will not listen.
questions: What do I owe to myself and to the world?
Where do I already know the right thing to do but hesitate?
Which of my habits keeps my life upright?

23.intro: Square 23 in Leela is the Celestial plane, swarga-loka in Sanskrit: heaven. It is a paradise of thoughts and desires free from the lower vices, and it sits at the centre of the third row, the Theater of Karma. The arrow of Purification from square 10 lands here. Johari makes clear that heaven is a resting place on the way, not the way out.
meaning: Johari describes the Celestial plane as the third loka, linked to the element of fire. Here desire still exists, but it has risen to the level of thought, free of the cruder vices of the lower squares. The player enjoys a sense of goodness, beauty and reward. He adds that heaven is built on the scaffolding of dharma: it is the natural result of right living.

The Sanskrit swarga-loka is the heavenly world of Indian cosmology, the realm of Indra and the gods, where those who have done good enjoy the fruit of their merit. It is the third step on the board's spine of lokas, after bhu-loka at 5 and bhuvar-loka at 14, at the heart of the Manipura chakra. Its element is fire, which here becomes light rather than heat.

The key word is temporary. In Indian thought swarga is real, yet merit runs out, and those who enjoy it return to the mortal world. The board says the same thing: square 23 lies in the third row, far from 68, Cosmic consciousness. A player who rises here quickly through Purification can mistake comfort for completion. Square 23 teaches the player to enjoy a good state without making it the goal, and to keep moving.
23.board: Square 23 is the central square of row 3, the Theater of Karma, and the tail of an arrow: Purification at square 10 lifts a player straight here from the second row. Players also arrive by an ordinary throw. Square 23 itself has no arrow or snake, so you stay here until the next throw. Just ahead, square 24, Bad company, is a snake down to 7 Conceit.
23.gita: Gita 9.20 teaches that heaven is real but temporary: when merit runs out, beings return to the mortal world. In the Mahabharata, Arjuna spends time in Indra's heaven, honoured and trained there, and then must return to earth to face the war.
questions: Where am I resting instead of moving on?
Which comfort have I mistaken for an arrival?
What good in my life is asking me to go further?

24.intro: Square 24 in Leela is Bad company, ku-sang-loka in Sanskrit, and it is a snake. Landing here sends the player from the third row down to square 7, Conceit, in the first row. Johari describes it as company out of accord with dharma: groups that swell the ego and selfishness. It is the only snake in the Theater of Karma.
meaning: Johari places Bad company right after the Celestial plane. A player who has tasted heaven can feel secure, and that is exactly when the wrong circle does its work. Bad company is not simply people who do wrong; it is any group whose values pull away from dharma, where flattery, rivalry and self-interest become normal. Ego swells, and the player starts to believe the story the group tells about them.

The Sanskrit ku-sang-loka means the world of bad association: ku is bad, sang (sanga) is company, association, and also attachment. The same word names both. We become attached to what our companions are attached to. Its counterpart is the next square, 25, su-sang-loka, Good company, the fellowship of seekers.

The snake falls a long way, from the Manipura chakra in the third row to square 7, Conceit, in the first row under Muladhara. Johari's reading is that inflated ego is not a higher state but a regression: it rebuilds castles in the air on the most basic insecurity. The square sits in the middle of the row with the strongest arrows, a reminder that the setting we choose matters as much as our own intentions. Square 24 teaches discernment about whom we let shape us.
24.board: Square 24 is the head of a snake in row 3, the Theater of Karma, right after the Celestial plane at 23. A player arrives by an ordinary throw; no arrow or snake from elsewhere ends here. Landing on 24 sends you straight down to square 7, Conceit, in row 1. It is the only snake in the third row, which also holds three arrows: Charity (20), Dharma (22) and Selfless service (27).
24.gita: Gita 2.62 traces the chain from attachment, sanga, which also means company, to desire and from desire to anger; you start living by what your circle lives by. In the Mahabharata, Shakuni's dice at the gambling match show how one person's influence can lead a whole family to ruin.
questions: Who is around me, and where are they taking me?
Whose approval am I chasing, and what does it cost me?
Which people help me become more honest with myself?

25.intro: Square 25 in Leela is Good company, su-sang-loka in Sanskrit. It stands for a fellowship of seekers, often gathered around a teacher, who act as mirrors for one another. It sits in the third row, the Theater of Karma, right after the snake of Bad company, and Harish Johari reads it as safe ground on the way to the heart.
meaning: Harish Johari describes Good company as the fellowship of people who are looking for the same thing. Such a circle often forms around a teacher, but its real work happens between the members: each one reflects the others, so habits and blind spots become visible without anyone having to point at them. Johari adds that from here “there are no more traps to bar his way to the fourth level.”

The Sanskrit name su-sang-loka joins su, good, with sang, company or association, and loka, plane. Its mirror image is square 24, ku-sang-loka, Bad company, where the same need for belonging turns sour and a snake drops the player to Conceit at 7. The two squares stand side by side for a reason: the board shows that the people around you can pull you down or hold you up.

Good company belongs to the Theater of Karma, the row of Manipura, the navel chakra of fire, where the player looks for identity and power and first becomes aware of karma. In that search for a self, the square teaches that identity is shaped in relationship. A good circle does not flatter; it reflects. It also makes the next steps of the row, sorrow and service, easier to carry.
25.board: Good company is a plain square: no arrow and no snake starts or ends here. A player reaches it by an ordinary throw from the squares just below it in row 3, often having just slipped past the snake of Bad company at 24. From 25 the next throw matters: a 2 lands on Selfless service (27) and its arrow to 41, a 3 on Apt religion (28) and its arrow to 50, and a 4 on Irreligiosity (29), whose snake falls to 6.
25.gita: The verse for this square is Gita 4.34: seek one who knows, come with humility, questions and service, and the truth will be shown to you. Its Mahabharata echo is Arjuna choosing Krishna over his army, a seeker preferring the right company to strength in numbers.
questions: Who supports me on my path?
Whose company leaves me clearer, and whose leaves me smaller?
What do I bring to the people who walk beside me?

26.intro: Square 26 in Leela is Sorrow, dukh in Sanskrit. It is the contraction of the heart that follows a loss, the low mood in which a player senses something higher yet feels unworthy of it. Harish Johari does not leave it there: the next square is Selfless service, and he says plainly that it offers hope.
meaning: Johari describes Sorrow as contraction and depression after loss. What makes it painful in the game is not only the loss itself but a particular feeling that comes with it: the player has begun to sense the Divine and feels unworthy of it. Grief here is the sorrow of someone who has glimpsed more than he can yet hold.

Dukh is the ordinary Sanskrit word for suffering, pain and unhappiness, the opposite of sukh, happiness, which the board places far above at square 62. On the Leela board sorrow is not a snake. It carries no punishment and sends no one down. It is a state to pass through, and Johari points straight past it: “Selfless service, the next square, offers hope.” Seen this way, sorrow is honest. It shows what mattered, and it does not need to be hurried away or hidden behind cheerfulness.

Sorrow belongs to the Theater of Karma, the third row, linked to Manipura, the navel chakra of fire. In a row about identity and power, sorrow is the moment the ego's plans meet loss. The teaching is gentle and practical: grief softens the hold of self-importance, and the way out runs through turning toward others rather than further inward.
26.board: Sorrow is a plain square in row 3, with no arrow or snake beginning or ending here; a player arrives by an ordinary throw from the squares below. What follows is striking. A throw of 1 lands on Selfless service (27), whose arrow lifts the player to the Human plane at 41. A 2 reaches the arrow of Apt religion (28) to 50, a 3 the snake of Irreligiosity (29) down to 6, and a 6 lands on the Plane of balance at 32.
26.gita: Its verse is Gita 1.47, where the Gita itself begins in grief: Arjuna drops his bow, his mind broken by sorrow, and Krishna answers gently that the wise grieve neither for the living nor the dead. The Mahabharata episode is Yudhishthira's grief after the war, sorrow that remains even in victory.
questions: What is my heart aching over?
What did this loss show me about what I hold dear?
Whom could I help today, even in a small way?

27.intro: Square 27 in Leela is Selfless service, parmarth in Sanskrit, and it is the base of an arrow. Working for something higher with no thought of reward lifts the player from the third row straight to square 41, the Human plane. Harish Johari stresses that service here is an inner attitude rather than a particular act.
meaning: For Johari, Selfless service means working for the supreme without concern for reward. He is careful to describe it as an attitude, not a deed: the same task can be service or self-promotion depending on what moves it. What counts is that the doer stops keeping accounts and lets the work belong to something larger than himself. Even small gestures count when they are offered this way, and large ones count for little when they are a bid for recognition.

Parmarth combines param, the highest or supreme, with artha, aim, purpose or meaning. It is action whose purpose lies beyond the self. In the game it closes the third row, the Theater of Karma, which is linked to Manipura, the navel chakra of fire. That row is about identity and power, and it ends with the one quality that dissolves the need for both.

Johari writes that the human plane “is often gained directly from the third chakra by the arrow of selfless service.” The arrow skips the whole fourth row and lands in the fifth, the row he titles Man Becomes Himself. The teaching is simple to state and hard to live: one becomes truly human by forgetting oneself in service, and that shortcut is open to anyone at any moment.
27.board: Selfless service is the base of one of the game's strongest arrows: landing on 27 carries the player at once from row 3 to square 41, the Human plane in row 5. A player gets here by an ordinary throw, for example a 1 from Sorrow (26), a 2 from Good company (25), a 4 from the Celestial plane (23) or a 6 from Atonement (21). No snake leads to this square.
27.gita: The square is paired with Gita 3.9: action done as an offering does not bind, so serve the wholeness of the world rather than a reward, as Krishna himself serves while needing nothing. Its Mahabharata image is Krishna acting as Arjuna's charioteer, a god taking the humble seat of service.
questions: Whom does my work really serve?
Where am I still waiting for thanks or credit?
What could I do today with no one ever knowing?

28.intro: Square 28 in Leela is Apt religion, sudharma in Sanskrit, and it is the base of an arrow. It means following your own dharma, living in tune with the laws of the game rather than someone else's rules. It opens the fourth row, Attaining Balance, and its arrow carries the player directly to square 50, the Plane of austerity.
meaning: Johari defines Apt religion as one's own dharma: living in harmony with the laws of the game. The emphasis falls on the word own. This is not a creed adopted from outside or a practice copied because it works for others. It is the way of life and the discipline that actually fit your nature, your stage and your duties. What suits one seeker can be a burden to another, and the game respects that difference.

Sudharma joins su, good or right, with dharma, the order that holds things together and the duty that follows from it. The board contrasts it with its neighbour: square 29, Irreligiosity, adharma, is blind faith that ignores cosmic law, and its snake falls to Delusion at 6. The two lie side by side, and between them sits the whole question of how a person relates to faith and practice.

Apt religion is the first square of the row Johari calls Attaining Balance, linked to Anahata, the heart chakra of air. In the heart, religion stops being a set of outer rules and becomes alignment with what is true for you. Johari writes that “sudharma leads him to the plane of austerity... directly to the sixth row”: the right practice makes real effort possible.
28.board: Apt religion is an arrow base: landing on 28 lifts the player at once from row 4 to square 50, the Plane of austerity in row 6. Because rows alternate direction, 28 sits directly above Selfless service (27) at the end of the third row. A player arrives by an ordinary throw, for example a 2 from Sorrow (26), a 3 from Good company (25) or a 5 from the Celestial plane (23).
28.gita: Its verse is Gita 3.35: better your own dharma done imperfectly than another's done well, so follow your own nature and your path will be true. The Mahabharata episode is the righteous butcher of Mithila, a humble tradesman whose faithful performance of his own duty made him a teacher of dharma.
questions: Which practice do I genuinely need?
Which rules am I following only because others follow them?
What would it look like to live my own dharma this week, imperfectly?

29.intro: Square 29 in Leela is Irreligiosity, adharma in Sanskrit, and it is the head of a snake. It stands for blind faith that ignores the laws of the game, belief without understanding. Landing here sends the player from the fourth row, the row of the heart, all the way down to square 6, Delusion, which Johari calls the start of the game.
meaning: Johari's Irreligiosity is not a lack of belief. It is belief that has lost its understanding: blind faith that ignores cosmic law, rules followed without seeing what they are for. He also describes it as an imbalance of the gunas, the three qualities of nature, so that action no longer fits the moment. It is acting against oneself while feeling right. From outside it can look like devotion; from inside it often feels like certainty.

Adharma is the negation of dharma, the a- of Sanskrit turning order into its absence. On the board it sits right beside square 28, Apt religion, sudharma, which is the arrow of one's own dharma. The pairing is precise: the same impulse toward faith either becomes a practice that fits you and rises to 50, or hardens into a rigid creed and falls. The board also pairs it with the arrow of the Plane of dharma at 22.

Irreligiosity lies in the fourth row, Attaining Balance, linked to Anahata, the heart chakra of air. A fall from the heart is a sharp lesson: even a player who has come this far can lose the thread if faith stops listening. Johari says of it, “It is a snake that takes one back to delusion, back to the start of the game.”
29.board: Irreligiosity is a snake head in row 4: landing on 29 drops the player at once to square 6, Delusion, in the first row. It is the only snake in the fourth row, and it falls three rows. Square 6 is also where every player first enters the game, which is why Johari speaks of a return to the start. A player reaches 29 by a throw such as a 3 from Sorrow (26), a 4 from Good company (25) or a 6 from the Celestial plane (23).
29.gita: The verse is Gita 4.7: Krishna comes whenever adharma rises, so when you see truth trampled, remember that lawlessness never has the last word. The Mahabharata episode is the attempt to disrobe Draupadi, adharma at its most naked, and the moment it fails.
questions: Where am I acting against myself?
Which of my beliefs have I never actually examined?
Where do I follow a rule while ignoring what it was meant to protect?

30.intro: Square 30 in Leela is Good tendencies, uttam gati in Sanskrit. It stands for the sound habits that arise on their own once there is inner balance: living with the rhythm of the day, eating well, breathing well. It sits in the fourth row, Attaining Balance, just past the snake of Irreligiosity, and it is a plain square with no arrow or snake.
meaning: Johari describes Good tendencies as spontaneous right habits that come from inner balance. He names them concretely: following the rhythms of sunrise and sunset, a suitable diet, asanas and pranayama. The key word is spontaneous. These are not rules imposed by willpower but the habits a balanced person falls into naturally, the way a calm body finds its own rhythm.

Uttam means best or highest, and gati means movement, course or tendency, the direction in which a life naturally flows. Uttam gati is the best course, the momentum of a life that has found its footing. Where the previous square, Irreligiosity, showed faith cut off from understanding, this one shows understanding showing up in the body and in daily routine. Johari's examples are not a regime to adopt in one day. They describe what tends to appear when the inner life is in order.

Good tendencies belongs to the fourth row, linked to Anahata, the heart chakra of air. In Johari's map the lower desires quiet down here, and energy is free to be used well. The teaching is modest and practical: balance becomes visible in ordinary things. One steady habit, kept gently, often does more for the path than a dramatic resolution.
30.board: Good tendencies is a plain square: no arrow or snake starts or ends here. A player reaches it by an ordinary throw, a 4 from Sorrow (26) or a 5 from Good company (25). It opens the calmest stretch of the board. From 30 every throw from 1 to 6 lands on squares 31 to 36, all in the heart row and none of them a snake, so the player is free to move through sanctity, balance, fragrance, taste, purgatory and clarity.
30.gita: Its verse is Gita 6.16: yoga is not for one who eats or sleeps too much or too little, and moderation in food, rest, work and sleep makes the path easy. The Mahabharata episode is Arjuna learning to shoot in the dark, a skill made natural by steady daily practice.
questions: Which simple habit would change my day?
Where do I swing between too much and too little?
Which part of my day already has a good rhythm, and how can I protect it?

31.intro: Square 31 in Leela is the Plane of sanctity, yaksha-loka in Sanskrit. It is the point where the divine stops being an idea and becomes lived experience, through understanding of cosmic principles. It lies in the fourth row, Attaining Balance, beside the Plane of balance at 32, and it is a plain square with no arrow or snake.
meaning: Johari describes the Plane of sanctity as divine grace experienced through understanding of cosmic principles. The emphasis is on experience. Before this point the sacred may have been a belief, a hope or a rule; here it becomes something felt and recognised. The understanding that opens the door is not a theory but a sense of how life is ordered, which makes grace perceptible in everyday events.

Yaksha-loka is the plane of the yakshas, nature spirits of Indian tradition associated with trees, waters and hidden treasure, guardians who stand between the human and the divine. In Leela the name marks a threshold of the sacred: a place where the subtle becomes present and approachable, and where reverence comes naturally rather than by effort.

The square belongs to the row of Anahata, the heart chakra of air. In the heart, knowing and feeling meet, and this is what lets grace be received. Coming right after Good tendencies, it suggests an order the player can test in life: steady habits clear the ground, and understanding then lets grace be noticed where it was always present. Sanctity here is not reserved for temples. It can be felt in a conversation, a kind act or a quiet hour, whenever the heart is open.
31.board: The Plane of sanctity is a plain square in row 4, with no arrow or snake beginning or ending here. A player arrives by an ordinary throw, a 1 from Good tendencies (30), a 5 from Sorrow (26) or a 6 from Good company (25). From 31, a throw of 1 to 5 stays in the heart row, while a 6 lands on True awareness (37), whose arrow lifts the player to the Plane of bliss at 66.
31.gita: Its verse is Gita 10.10: to those devoted and full of love, Krishna gives the understanding that leads to him, and grace becomes living experience when you listen with the heart. The Mahabharata episode is the Yaksha's questions, in which a yaksha tests Yudhishthira at a lake and wise answers restore life.
questions: Where do I feel grace?
What in my life feels sacred without needing an explanation?
When did I last listen with the heart rather than the mind?

32.intro: Square 32 in Leela is the Plane of balance, maha- or mahar-loka in Sanskrit. It is the heart of the board: the fourth of the lokas on the central column, where the desires of the lower chakras quiet down and energy begins to flow upward. The arrow of Charity rises here from square 20, and the square itself is a resting place.
meaning: Johari describes the Plane of balance as the fourth loka, where the desires of the lower chakras are stilled and an upward flow begins from the heart. The first three rows were about survival, fantasy and power. Here those pulls have not disappeared, but they no longer run the player. With the lower desires quiet, energy is free to rise.

Mahar-loka, also written maha-loka, is the fourth of the seven lokas, the planes of existence in Indian cosmology. On the Leela board these planes form what Johari calls the spine of the game board: the central column of 5, 14, 23, 32, 41, 50, 59 and 68. Square 32 sits exactly in the middle of that column, as the heart sits between the lower and upper body.

The square gives its centre to the fourth row, Attaining Balance, linked to Anahata, the heart chakra of air. Johari says it is reached “through the arrow of charity.” The teaching is that balance is not a static midpoint but the result of giving: when one stops grasping, the heart settles, and steadiness follows as a natural consequence. On a board that keeps lifting and dropping the player, this square is a reminder that steadiness itself is a place one can return to.
32.board: The Plane of balance is the tip of an arrow: a player who lands on Charity (20) in row 3 is carried up here at once. It can also be reached by an ordinary throw, a 1 from the Plane of sanctity (31), a 2 from Good tendencies (30) or a 6 from Sorrow (26). No snake leaves 32. From here a 5 lands on True awareness (37), whose arrow rises to the Plane of bliss at 66.
32.gita: Its verse is Gita 2.48: evenness of mind is yoga, so meet pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike, and you will find steadiness. The Mahabharata episode is Bhishma on the bed of arrows, lying pierced yet calm, teaching dharma from the centre of his pain.
questions: What would bring me back into balance?
Which pull from below still decides for me without my noticing?
What could I give away, in time, attention or things, to steady my heart?

33.intro: Square 33 in Leela is the Plane of fragrance, gandha-loka in Sanskrit. Here the senses are refined: smell, the sense of the earth element, is transformed into a subtle and pleasing fragrance, and even the body's odours are purified. It lies in the fourth row, Attaining Balance, just after the Plane of balance, and it is a plain square with no arrow or snake.
meaning: Johari describes the Plane of fragrance as the place where smell is transmuted into divine fragrance and the body's odours are purified. It is the first of two squares in the heart row about refined senses. The point is not to give the senses up but to let them become finer, so that what once drew the player down into craving now becomes a way of perceiving beauty.

Gandha is Sanskrit for smell or fragrance, and loka means plane. In Indian thought smell is tied to the earth element and to the first chakra, the very beginning of the board. Meeting it again at square 33, purified, shows the movement of the whole game: the same energy that began as basic survival returns, in the heart, as delicacy and appreciation.

Fragrance follows balance on the board for a reason. Once the lower desires have quietened at square 32, the senses no longer need to grab. They can simply receive. The teaching is practical and close at hand: a player can notice what actually nourishes the senses today, rather than what merely stimulates them, and let attention become as light as a scent. Even a single breath of a familiar scent can be enough to bring the mind home.
33.board: The Plane of fragrance is a plain square in row 4, with no arrow or snake beginning or ending here. A player arrives by an ordinary throw, a 1 from the Plane of balance (32), a 2 from the Plane of sanctity (31) or a 3 from Good tendencies (30). From 33, a throw of 4 lands on True awareness (37), whose arrow rises to the Plane of bliss at 66; the other throws stay in the heart row or move into row 5.
33.gita: Its verse is Gita 7.9, where Krishna is the pure fragrance of the earth: learn to notice the Divine in simple things, the smell of rain, a flower, a fresh morning. The Mahabharata episode is Bhima's search for the Saugandhika lotus, a journey set in motion by a single fragrant flower.
questions: What is nourishing my senses today?
Which smell or small sensation brings me back to the present?
Where do I seek stimulation when what I need is something subtler?

34.intro: Square 34 in Leela is the Plane of taste, rasa-loka in Sanskrit. Taste here is meant in the aesthetic sense of rasa: the essence of emotion and poetry, the flavour of an experience fully felt. It lies in the fourth row, Attaining Balance, after the Plane of fragrance, and it is a plain square with no arrow or snake.
meaning: Johari treats the Plane of taste as taste in the aesthetic sense: rasa, the essence of emotion and poetry. He adds that refined taste draws admirers. A person whose perception has become fine radiates something others recognise and are drawn to, not through display but through the quality of attention they bring to food, art, conversation and feeling.

Rasa has several layers in Sanskrit. It means juice or sap, the taste of food, and, in Indian aesthetics, the emotional flavour that a poem, a piece of music or a dance awakens in the one who receives it.
