Rasa-loka is the plane where these meanings meet. The tongue's taste, linked to the water element and the second chakra, returns here transformed into the capacity to savour life itself. Classical Indian theory names several rasas, such as love, wonder, compassion and peace, each a different way the heart can be moved.

Coming after Fragrance, this square completes the pair of refined senses in the heart row of Anahata, the heart chakra of air. The teaching is to refine taste rather than suppress it. A life of rasa is not a life of more pleasure but of deeper pleasure, where the player tastes each experience fully and needs less of it.
34.board: The Plane of taste is a plain square in row 4, with no arrow or snake beginning or ending here. A player arrives by an ordinary throw, a 1 from the Plane of fragrance (33), a 2 from the Plane of balance (32), a 3 from the Plane of sanctity (31) or a 4 from Good tendencies (30). From 34, a throw of 3 lands on True awareness (37), whose arrow rises to the Plane of bliss at 66.
34.gita: Its verse is Gita 7.8, where Krishna is the taste of water: the craving for sense objects fades only once you have tasted the Highest, so refine your taste rather than suppress it. The Mahabharata episode is Arjuna living as Brihannala, the great warrior teaching dance and music at the court of Virata.
questions: What does my life taste like right now?
What experience have I rushed through without really tasting it?
Where could I take less and savour more?

35.intro: Square 35 in Leela is Purgatory, narka-loka in Sanskrit. It means bearing the consequences of freely chosen actions and accepting them without judgement, as a sign that something can be improved. It lies in the fourth row, Attaining Balance, and it is where the snake of the Plane of violence at 52 delivers a fallen player.
meaning: Johari describes Purgatory as bearing the consequences of actions one has freely chosen. What makes the square distinctive is how those consequences are seen. In the fourth chakra they appear “as the sign of an imperfection of action and the need to improve,” without valuation. There is no verdict here and no condemnation, only an honest look at results and a willingness to learn from them.

Narka, more often written naraka, is the Sanskrit word for hell, and loka means plane. Yet the board places this hell in the heart row, beside taste and clarity, not at the bottom of the game. That placement is the lesson: suffering that follows our own choices is not eternal punishment but a stage, and accepting responsibility for it is what opens the way forward.

Purgatory belongs to the row of Anahata, the heart chakra of air. Only a heart that has found some balance can look at its own mistakes without collapsing into guilt or hardening into defence. The square asks for responsibility rather than blame, and the next square, Clarity of consciousness, shows what such honesty makes possible. Seen this way, purgatory is less a sentence than a workshop, where action is examined and refined. It is temporary by nature.
35.board: Purgatory is the tail of a snake: a player who lands on the Plane of violence (52) in row 6 falls here at once, two rows down. Johari calls it the fourth-chakra purgatory where the player must atone. It can also be reached by an ordinary throw from the squares just before it in row 4, from Good tendencies (30) to the Plane of taste (34). No arrow or snake starts on 35, and a throw of 2 from here reaches True awareness (37) and its arrow to 66.
35.gita: Its verse is Gita 16.16: caught in the net of delusion, people fall into hell, and desire, anger and greed are its gates; hell is not eternal punishment but the result of a choice you can change. The Mahabharata episode is Yudhishthira's vision of hell, which proves to be a passing illusion.
questions: What am I ready to take responsibility for?
Which consequence am I still treating as a punishment rather than a lesson?
What one change would show that I have learned from it?

36.intro: Square 36 in Leela is Clarity of consciousness, swatch in Sanskrit. It is the transparency that follows purgatory: the fog of the intellect lifts and is replaced by clear inner feeling. It is the last square of the fourth row, Attaining Balance, and the passage to the fifth row, and it is a plain square with no arrow or snake.
meaning: Johari describes Clarity of consciousness as transparency after purgatory. The fog of intellect, the endless weighing and arguing of the mind, is replaced by clear inner feeling. This is not cleverness. It is the simple seeing that comes once one has accepted the consequences of one's actions and no longer needs to defend or explain them. Johari places it at the end of the heart row, where feeling has been refined by balance, fragrance and taste.

Swatch, often written svaccha, means clear, transparent or pure, like clean water through which the bottom can be seen. The image fits: consciousness here is not filled with new content but emptied of murk. What was always there becomes visible, and the player knows what he feels and what he needs to do without long deliberation. Nothing new has to be added for clarity to come; something only has to settle.

The square closes the heart row of Anahata, the heart chakra of air, and Johari calls it the transition to the fifth row. Its place right after Purgatory carries the teaching: honesty about one's actions is followed by lightness. Clarity is not the reward for being perfect but the natural result of no longer hiding from oneself.
36.board: Clarity of consciousness is a plain square at the end of row 4, with no arrow or snake beginning or ending here. Players reach it by an ordinary throw from any square between Good tendencies (30) and Purgatory (35). Because rows alternate direction, 36 sits directly below True awareness (37), and a throw of 1 lands there, on an arrow that rises to the Plane of bliss at 66. A 5 reaches the Human plane at 41.
36.gita: Its verse is Gita 18.73, where at the end Arjuna says that his delusion is gone, his memory restored, his doubts ended; when ignorance is dispelled, knowledge shines like the sun. The Mahabharata episode is Sanjaya's divine sight, the gift of seeing the whole battlefield clearly from afar.
questions: What has become clear?
What do I know in my heart that my mind keeps arguing with?
What is the next simple step this clarity points to?

37.intro: Square 37 in Leela is True awareness, gyana (jnana in Sanskrit), the first square of the fifth row. It stands for knowing what is right and seeing how to live it. Landing here sends the player up an arrow to square 66, the plane of bliss, one of four arrows on the board that end in the top row.
meaning: Harish Johari describes gyana as knowledge of the right together with insight into how to live it. It is not book learning or a store of facts. It is the moment when understanding becomes clear enough to shape how you act, speak and choose.

The Sanskrit jnana comes from the root jna, to know, the same root behind the English word know. In Indian thought it names knowing that transforms the knower. Johari adds an important caution: gyana is not liberation. It carries the player very high, to the plane of bliss, but it does not by itself end the game. Knowledge opens the door; living it is another matter.

Square 37 opens row 5, which Johari calls Man Becomes Himself and links to Vishuddha, the throat chakra, whose element is ether. The throat is the centre of expression, where what is understood inwardly can be voiced. It fits that this row begins with true awareness: the player who has crossed the heart row now knows something real and must decide what to do with it.
The square teaches the gap between knowing and doing. Most people already know more than they practise. Gyana asks you to notice that gap honestly, without guilt, and to close it one step at a time.
37.board: Square 37 is the first square of row 5. Players usually reach it with a throw from the heart row, from squares 31 to 36, the last stretch of the fourth row. No arrow or snake ends here. On landing, the arrow of gyana lifts the player at once from row 5 to row 8 and square 66, the plane of bliss.
37.gita: The verse for this square is Gita 4.38: nothing in this world is as pure as knowledge, and one full of faith who masters the senses gains it and soon reaches the highest peace. Its episode is the Anugita, where Arjuna admits he has forgotten the teaching and Krishna must give it again, a reminder that knowledge fades unless it is lived.
questions: What do I already know but fail to apply?
Which piece of understanding have I received more than once without acting on it?
What would one small step of living what I know look like today?

38.intro: Square 38 in Leela is the Plane of life energy, prana-loka. It stands for prana, the life force carried by the in-breath, which keeps the body in balance. It is a plain square in the fifth row, with no arrow and no snake, and it invites the player to notice what truly gives them vitality.
meaning: Johari describes square 38 simply: prana, the life force and in-breath, balances the body. In yoga, prana is both the breath you draw and the subtle energy that animates every living thing. Breathing in is the most constant act of receiving that a body performs.

Prana-loka means the plane or world of prana. It is the first of three neighbouring squares devoted to the vital airs: prana at 38, apana at 39 and vyana at 40. Together they describe how life enters, leaves and circulates. Johari places them here because in row 5 the vital airs come into balance.

Row 5 is Man Becomes Himself, linked to Vishuddha, the throat chakra, with ether as its element. The throat is where breath becomes voice. After the arrow of true awareness at square 37, this square brings the player back to the body. Insight needs energy to be lived, and energy depends on how one breathes, rests, eats and spends attention.

The lesson is quiet and practical. Vitality is not only a matter of effort. It grows when you notice what nourishes you and what drains you, and when you let the breath become something you feel rather than something that happens unseen.
38.board: Square 38 sits in row 5, just after square 37. Players arrive by a throw from squares 32 to 36; anyone landing on 37 is carried away by its arrow. No arrow or snake leads here, and none leaves. It is a plain square: the player stays, reflects on vitality and moves on with the next throw.
38.gita: The square is linked to Gita 4.29, where some offer the in-breath into the out-breath and the out-breath into the in-breath, so that breathing itself becomes an inner offering. Its episode is Bhima's meeting with Hanuman, both sons of Vayu, the wind, and so of the breath of life.
questions: What gives me vitality?
What drains my energy without my noticing?
How does my breathing change when I am calm, and when I am under pressure?

39.intro: Square 39 in Leela is the Plane of elimination, apana-loka. It represents apana, the downward air of the body that carries away what is no longer needed. Johari teaches that bringing it into harmony rejuvenates. It is a plain square in the fifth row, asking the player what it is time to release.
meaning: In Johari's commentary, apana is the downward air of elimination, and harmonising it rejuvenates. Yoga describes several vital airs, each with its own direction. Apana moves down and out: it governs exhalation, cleansing and everything the body sets aside so that it can stay healthy.

Apana-loka means the plane of apana. It follows square 38, the plane of prana, and the pairing is deliberate. Prana brings life in; apana makes room for it by letting go. A body that only takes in and never releases cannot stay in balance, and the same is true of a mind or a life.

The square belongs to row 5, Man Becomes Himself, linked to Vishuddha, the throat chakra, whose element is ether. Ether is space, and this square is about creating space. Before the player can become fully themselves in this row, something old has to be allowed to leave: a habit, a grudge, a role, an outdated picture of who they are.

The teaching is that release is not loss. Renewal depends on it. Square 39 invites you to look at what you are still carrying out of habit and to let it go without drama, the way an out-breath leaves the body.
39.board: Square 39 is in row 5, between 38 Life energy and 40 Circulation. Players reach it by a throw from the squares below, from 33 to 38, except 37, whose arrow carries a player away. No arrow or snake ends here and none starts here, so it is a plain square. The player remains for the turn, considers what to release, and continues with the next throw of the die.
39.gita: Gita 4.29 is the verse for this square: prana and apana are offered into each other, and letting go is as sacred as receiving. Its episode is the quarrel of the five vital breaths, in which each breath claims to matter most until all see that the body depends on their cooperation.
questions: What is it time for me to release?
What do I keep holding on to only because it is familiar?
What new thing could enter if I made room for it?

40.intro: Square 40 in Leela is the Plane of circulation, vyana-loka. It represents vyana, the vital air that distributes prana through the whole body, as in circulation and sweating. It is a plain square in the fifth row, without arrow or snake, and it asks the player where their energy is actually flowing.
meaning: Johari describes vyana as the air that distributes prana, the work we see in circulation and sweating. After prana brings life in at square 38 and apana carries the waste away at square 39, vyana spreads what has been received to every limb and organ. Without it, energy would gather in one place and leave the rest starved.

Vyana-loka means the plane of vyana. The Sanskrit vyana suggests something that moves outward and pervades. It completes the trio of vital airs that Johari places together in the fifth row, where the airs are brought into balance as the player matures.

Row 5 is Man Becomes Himself, linked to Vishuddha, the throat chakra, whose element is ether, the space in which everything moves. Square 40 sits just before 41, the Human plane at the centre of the row. A person on the way to becoming fully human needs not only energy but its even distribution: attention given to work, relationships, body and inner life, rather than poured into one channel.

The teaching is about flow. Energy is not only something you have; it is something that goes somewhere. Square 40 invites you to trace where your strength actually travels each day, and where it no longer reaches.
40.board: Square 40 is in row 5, between 39 Elimination and 41 the Human plane. Players arrive with a throw from the squares below, from 34 to 39, except the arrow base at 37. No arrow or snake leads here and none leaves, so it is a plain square. The player stays for the turn, reflects on where their energy flows, and moves on with the next throw.
40.gita: The verse is Gita 15.13, where Krishna enters the earth and sustains all beings with his strength, so that life flows through each person like blood through the body. Its episode is again the quarrel of the five vital breaths, which shows that every part of the body lives only when the breaths work together.
questions: Where is my energy flowing?
Which part of my life has stopped receiving my attention?
Where am I pouring in more strength than the situation needs?

41.intro: Square 41 in Leela is the Human plane, jana-loka, the central square of the fifth row and the fifth of the seven lokas that form the spine of the board. Johari calls it the abode of sages and saints, where the player gains a true perspective on humanity and may become a teacher. The arrow from square 27 lands here.
meaning: Johari describes jana-loka as the fifth loka, the abode of siddhas and saints. Here the player gains a true perspective on humanity and may become a teacher or seer. It is a place of maturity: the player has seen enough of karma, balance and loss to understand people as they are, with compassion rather than judgement.

Jana means people, or the born, and loka means world or plane. Jana-loka is the world of those who have become fully human. It is one of the seven lokas that run up the central column of the board, from 5 Bhu-loka through 14, 23 and 32 to 41, then on to 50, 59 and finally 68. Each loka marks the heart of its row.

Row 5, Man Becomes Himself, is linked to Vishuddha, the throat chakra. Johari maps this row onto the years 28 to 35 of life, the stage of the teacher. The throat is the centre of speech, and a teacher is someone whose understanding has found its voice.
The square teaches that what you have lived can be passed on. It also carries a caution: the Human plane is a high station, but it is not the goal. Teaching others does not end one's own journey.
41.board: Square 41 is the middle square of row 5 and sits on the central spine of the board. One arrow ends here: the arrow of Selfless service from square 27, which lifts a player from row 3 straight to the Human plane. Others arrive by a throw from squares 35 to 40, except the arrow base at 37. Square 41 has no arrow or snake of its own, so play continues normally.
41.gita: The verse is Gita 8.16: all worlds up to Brahma's lead back to return, so even the high human state is a station and not the final goal. Its episode is Markandeya's teachings in the forest, where the ageless sage instructs the exiled Pandavas, an image of the teacher this square describes.
questions: What could I teach?
What have I learned through experience that others around me are still struggling with?
Where am I tempted to treat a high point as the end of the road?

42.intro: Square 42 in Leela is the Plane of fire, agni-loka. Johari describes Agni, fire, as the cycle in which the divine essence is reborn, and says the player here is ready to assume form. It is a plain square in the fifth row, inviting reflection on what in you is ready to burn away and begin again.
meaning: For Johari, square 42 shows Agni as the cycle of rebirth of the divine essence. At this point the player is ready to assume form. Fire is the great transformer: it turns wood into heat, light and ash, and in Indian ritual it carries offerings from the human world to the divine.

Agni is both the Sanskrit word for fire and the name of the fire deity, one of the oldest in the Vedas. Agni-loka is the plane of fire. Fire appears earlier in the game as the element of the third chakra, where it fuels ambition and karma. Here, in the fifth row, it has a different role: it no longer drives desire but refines the person, burning what has had its day so that something truer can take shape.

The square sits in row 5, Man Becomes Himself, linked to Vishuddha, the throat chakra. It comes right after the Human plane at 41 and right before 43, Birth of man. The sequence is telling: perspective, then purifying fire, then a new birth.
Square 42 teaches that transformation asks for something to be given up. Fire does not negotiate. What you are willing to let burn decides what can be born.
42.board: Square 42 is in row 5, between 41 the Human plane and 43 Birth of man. Players reach it with a throw from the squares below, from 36 to 41 (except the arrow base at 37), and those lifted to 41 by the arrow from 27 may arrive here on their next throw. No arrow or snake begins or ends on 42, so it is a plain square.
42.gita: The verse is Gita 4.37: as fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge burns up all karma. Its episode is the birth of Draupadi from the sacrificial fire of King Drupada, a figure who emerges fully formed from the flame.
questions: What in me is ready to burn away and be born again?
Which old way of seeing myself is costing me more than it gives?
What am I afraid to lose, and what might take its place?

43.intro: Square 43 in Leela is Birth of man, manushya-janma. Johari describes it as birth as a true human being, without caste, creed or nation, with reason in the service of truth. It is a plain square in the fifth row, and it asks the player a simple, searching question: what kind of person do I want to become?
meaning: Johari calls this square birth as a true Man, "son of God only", without caste, creed or nation. The player has been physically born at square 1, Genesis. Here a second birth takes place: the emergence of a person whose identity no longer rests on origin, status or group, and whose reason serves truth rather than self-interest.

Manushya means human, and janma means birth. The name echoes square 1, janma, but the meaning has deepened. At the start of the game birth was entry into karma. In row 5, birth is becoming fully human, a person who sees others as equals because the same Self lives in all.

The square belongs to row 5, Man Becomes Himself, linked to Vishuddha, the throat chakra. It follows 42, the Plane of fire, where the old was burned away, and precedes 44 Ignorance and 45 Right knowledge, a choice between forgetting and practice.

The teaching is that being human is not given by birth alone. It is something you grow into, through the way you think, choose and treat others. Square 43 invites you to picture the person you could become and to measure your present against that picture, kindly but honestly.
43.board: Square 43 sits in row 5, between 42 the Plane of fire and 44 Ignorance. Players reach it by a throw from the squares below, from 38 to 42; square 37 is an arrow base, so nobody stays there to throw. No arrow or snake begins or ends here, so it is a plain square. From 43 the next throw can carry the player onto the snake at 44 or the arrow at 45.
43.gita: The verse is Gita 5.18: the wise see the same Self in a brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste, so true human birth lies in clarity of sight rather than origin. Its episode is Karna at the tournament, where he is mocked for his supposed low birth despite his skill.
questions: What kind of person do I want to become?
Where do I still judge people by where they come from?
Does my reasoning serve the truth, or does it serve what I want to be true?

44.intro: Square 44 in Leela is Ignorance, avidya. Johari describes it as forgetting the illusory nature of existence and becoming attached to emotional states. It is a snake: landing here sends the player from the fifth row all the way down to square 9, the Sensual plane, in the first row. It sits right beside square 45, Right knowledge.
meaning: In Johari's words, ignorance is forgetting the illusory nature of existence and attaching to emotional states, and "this snake draws his energy down to the first chakra and the sensual plane." Avidya is not a lack of information. A player can reach row 5 with real understanding and still fall here, simply by forgetting what they know and letting feelings take the wheel.

Avidya combines a, not, with vidya, knowledge or seeing. It is not-seeing: the veil that makes passing states look solid and permanent. In Indian philosophy avidya is often named as the root of the other afflictions. Its opposite, suvidya, right knowledge, waits on the very next square, which makes 44 and 45 one of the clearest paired opposites on the board.

The square lies in row 5, Man Becomes Himself, linked to Vishuddha, the throat chakra. That such a long snake waits so high shows that progress offers no protection against forgetting. Johari's Sensual plane, square 9, is the plane of desire of every kind.
Square 44 teaches vigilance without fear. The fall is not a punishment. It shows what happens when attention lapses, and it points the way back: to notice, to wake up, and to look more closely.
44.board: Square 44 is in row 5, between 43 Birth of man and 45 Right knowledge. Players reach it by a throw from squares 38 to 43; no arrow or snake ends here. It is the head of a snake: landing on 44 sends the player from row 5 down to square 9, the Sensual plane, at the end of row 1.
44.gita: The verse is Gita 5.15: knowledge is veiled by ignorance, and so beings go astray. Its episode is Dhritarashtra refusing to hear Vidura, the blind king who keeps ignoring his wise counsellor's warnings.
questions: What do I prefer not to notice?
Which emotion do I let decide for me when I would rather not think?
What did I once understand clearly that I have since let myself forget?

45.intro: Square 45 in Leela is Right knowledge, suvidya, the last square of the fifth row. Johari describes it as awareness joined with practice. It is an arrow: landing here lifts the player from row 5 to square 67, the Plane of cosmic good, in the top row. As Johari puts it, the player is then one square away from the goal.
meaning: Johari writes that awareness plus practice "lifts the player to the eighth plane and the plane of cosmic good. He is now one square away from his goal." He adds that right knowledge protects from many snakes. It is knowledge that has been tested in life and found to hold.

Suvidya joins su, good or right, with vidya, knowledge. It is the direct answer to avidya, Ignorance, on the square just before it. Where avidya is forgetting, suvidya is remembering and practising. The contrast between 37 and 45 is also instructive: gyana at 37 is knowing what is right, while suvidya at 45 is that knowing carried into action.

Square 45 closes row 5, Man Becomes Himself, linked to Vishuddha, the throat chakra. Its arrow lands on 67, Rudra-loka, the abode of Shiva, next to the goal at 68. Johari notes that right knowledge stops one square short: only Spiritual devotion at 54 lands on 68 itself, a sign that knowledge alone does not complete the journey.

The teaching is that knowledge becomes right knowledge only when it is lived. Square 45 asks you to look for the places where your understanding and your behaviour still go separate ways. That is where the next step lies.
45.board: Square 45 is the last square of row 5. Players reach it by a throw from squares 39 to 43; anyone landing on 44 is carried down its snake. No arrow or snake ends here. On landing, the arrow of right knowledge lifts the player from row 5 to row 8 and square 67, the Plane of cosmic good.
45.gita: The verse is Gita 10.32, where Krishna says that among all sciences he is the knowledge of the Self, a knowledge that can be tested in experience. Its episode is the Yaksha's questions, in which Yudhishthira answers a spirit's riddles at a lake and saves his brothers through lived wisdom.
questions: Where do my knowledge and my actions part ways?
Which principle do I defend in words but rarely practise?
What have I tested in my own experience, rather than only read or heard?

46.intro: Square 46 in Leela is Conscience, vivek, the first square of the sixth row. Johari describes it as the inner wisdom that tells the subtle from the gross, the faculty of the third eye. It is an arrow: landing here lifts the player to square 62, Happiness, in the seventh row. In Johari's words, the player is immediately transported to happiness.
meaning: Johari describes vivek as inner wisdom discerning the subtle from the gross, the function of the third eye. "When the player lands on the square of conscience he is immediately transported to happiness." Conscience here is not a set of rules learned from outside. It is a clear inner sense of what is true and what is not.

Vivek, or viveka, means discrimination in the old sense of the word: the ability to distinguish. Indian traditions treat it as a key quality on the path, the power to separate the lasting from the passing and the essential from the superficial.

Square 46 opens row 6, which Johari calls The Time of Penance and links to Ajna, the third-eye chakra between the eyebrows. He maps this row onto the years 35 to 42, when a person becomes the observer of their own patterns. It fits that this row begins with conscience: the player who has become fully human in row 5 now learns to see and judge their own movements from within.
The teaching is that happiness follows from listening inwardly. Square 46 asks you to notice the quiet voice that already knows, and to give it as much weight as the louder voices around you.
46.board: Square 46 is the first square of row 6, reached by a throw from the end of row 5, from squares 40 to 43. Players landing on 44 or 45 are carried away by the snake or arrow there. No arrow or snake ends on 46. On landing, the arrow of conscience lifts the player from row 6 to square 62, Happiness, in row 7.
46.gita: The verse is Gita 18.30: sattvic understanding knows what to do and what not to do, what to fear and what not to fear, what binds and what frees. Its episode is Arjuna choosing Krishna, unarmed, over Krishna's whole army, a choice of the subtle over the gross.
questions: What is my conscience telling me?
When did I last ignore an inner signal, and what happened?
Which choice in front of me would look different if I judged it by its subtle effects?

47.intro: Square 47 in Leela is the Plane of neutrality, named Saraswati. Johari identifies it with sushumna, the neutral central channel of the subtle body, and describes it as going beyond the judgement of good and bad. It is a plain square in the sixth row, the first of three squares devoted to the subtle body's main channels.
meaning: Johari describes square 47 as sushumna, the neutral central channel, a state that goes beyond judging things as good or bad. Yoga pictures three main channels of subtle energy running along the spine: ida on the left, pingala on the right and sushumna in the middle. When energy flows through the central channel, the mind is neither pulled towards pleasure nor pushed away by pain.

The square is named Saraswati after the sacred river and the goddess of learning and speech. Row 6 assigns the three channels to three rivers: Saraswati for sushumna at 47, Yamuna for pingala at 48 and Ganga for ida at 49. In Indian tradition the Saraswati is the river that flows unseen, which suits a channel that cannot be observed directly.

The square sits in row 6, The Time of Penance, linked to Ajna, the third-eye chakra. After conscience at 46 learns to distinguish, neutrality at 47 learns to stop labelling. These are not in conflict: one sees clearly, the other does not add a verdict to what it sees.
The teaching is that much suffering comes from judgement layered on experience. Square 47 invites you to meet events as they are before deciding whether they are good or bad.
47.board: Square 47 sits in row 6, just after 46 Conscience. Players reach it by a throw from squares 41 to 43; those who land on 44, 45 or 46 are carried away by a snake or an arrow. No arrow or snake begins or ends here, so it is a plain square, and play continues with the next throw.
47.gita: The verse is Gita 2.48: act without attachment, the same in success and failure, for a mind settled in yoga leaves both good and bad behind. Its episode is Balarama's pilgrimage along the Sarasvati, taken when he refused to fight on either side of the great war.
questions: What would change if I stopped judging?
Which recent event did I label good or bad before I really understood it?
Can I act fully today while staying the same in success and failure?

48.intro: Square 48 in Leela is the Solar plane, named Yamuna. Johari identifies it with pingala, the right-hand, solar current of the subtle body, the energy of activity, will and clarity. It is a plain square in the sixth row. Balancing this solar current with the lunar one on square 49, Johari says, creates the witness-self.
meaning: Johari describes square 48 as pingala, the right-side, male and solar current. Balancing it with the lunar current creates the witness-self. Pingala is the heating, active side of the subtle body: it drives initiative, decision and outward action.

The square is named Yamuna, after the river that joins the Ganga at Prayag. In the row of the three channels, Yamuna stands for pingala, Saraswati at 47 for the neutral sushumna, and Ganga at 49 for ida, the lunar current. The Yamuna is also associated with Yama, her brother, and with Surya, the sun, her father, which suits the solar plane.

The square lies in row 6, The Time of Penance, linked to Ajna, the third-eye chakra, where the player observes their own patterns. Solar energy is valuable here, but not on its own. Too much of it becomes force and impatience; too little, and nothing gets done. Johari's point is balance: when the solar and lunar currents meet in equal measure, a calm witness appears who can act without being driven.
Square 48 teaches the right use of will. It asks where you hold back when action is needed, and where clear, decisive effort would serve you and others.
48.board: Square 48 is in row 6, between 47 Neutrality and 49 the Lunar plane. Players arrive by a throw from 42, 43 or 47; landing on 44, 45 or 46 carries a player away by a snake or an arrow. No arrow or snake begins or ends on 48. It is a plain square, and play continues with the next throw.
48.gita: The verse is Gita 10.21, where Krishna says that among lights he is the radiant sun, the light that fills the world. Its episode is Karna, son of Surya the sun god, a figure of great strength and generosity whose will was not always well directed.
questions: Where do I need to act more decisively?
Where does my drive turn into pressure on myself or on others?
What would balance my activity with rest and receptivity?

49.intro: Square 49 in Leela is the Lunar plane, named Ganga in Sanskrit. It stands for ida, the cool, receptive current on the left side of the subtle body. In Harish Johari's game of self-knowledge it marks the moment a player learns to receive and nourish, balancing the effort and heat of the solar side.
meaning: Johari describes the Lunar plane as ida, the left-side, feminine current of the subtle body: magnetic, cooling and nourishing. He links it to the yoga of nostril breathing, in which breath through the left nostril is felt as calming and inward. The square is not about doing more. It is about letting something be given back to you.

The Sanskrit name is Ganga, the sacred river that descends from the heavens and feeds the plains of India. In the board's symbolism, the three great rivers are the three channels of the subtle body: Saraswati at 47 is sushumna, the neutral centre; Yamuna at 48 is pingala, the solar current; Ganga at 49 is ida, the lunar one. Together they sit side by side in row 6.

Row 6, The Time of Penance, belongs to the Ajna chakra, the third eye, where the player works on discernment. Here the lunar square softens a row otherwise full of austerity and effort. Johari notes that balancing the solar and lunar currents gives rise to the witness self, the part of you that watches without being carried away.
What it teaches is simple and often neglected: receptivity is a strength. Care, rest and gentleness are part of inner work, not a pause from it.
49.board: Square 49 sits in row 6, The Time of Penance, between the Solar plane at 48 and the Plane of austerity at 50. No arrow or snake leads here, so a player arrives only by an ordinary throw from the squares just below. It is a plain square: there is no arrow to climb and no snake to fall, and on the next throw the player simply moves on by count.
49.gita: In Gita 15.13 Krishna says that, becoming the moon, he nourishes every plant with its sap, which is the lunar quality of this square. The story of Ganga and Shantanu shows the river goddess as a giver whose gifts come on her own terms, and who leaves when she is not trusted.
questions: Where do I need more gentleness?
What would I receive if I stopped pushing for a while?
Where in my life do I give care, and where do I allow myself to be cared for?

50.intro: Square 50 in Leela is the Plane of austerity, tapa-loka, the sixth of the seven lokas on the board's central spine. It stands for penance, sustained work on oneself and meditation. Players often reach it by the arrow from square 28, Apt religion, which Johari describes as one's own dharma lifting the player straight to the sixth row.
meaning: For Johari, tapa-loka is the plane of penance and hard work on the self. Tapas literally means heat: the inner heat produced by discipline, by staying with a practice when it is no longer easy. The player who reaches this square is not resting on talent but refining attention through effort and meditation.

Johari adds that the being of the sixth chakra reveals the Divine to others. Austerity here is not a private achievement or a display of willpower. Its fruit is a clarity that others can feel and use.

Square 50 is the central plane of row 6, The Time of Penance, and belongs to the Ajna chakra, the third eye. It sits on the spine of the board, the middle column that holds the lokas from 5 Bhu-loka to 68 Vaikuntha. That central place makes it the keynote of the whole row: every square around it is a form of penance, discernment or its risks.

The square also carries a warning. Two squares further on lies 52, the Plane of violence, where zeal turns hard. Austerity that becomes self-torment, or a reason to judge others, has lost its point. The lesson of square 50 is a discipline chosen freely, held with faith, and free of the need for reward.
50.board: Square 50 sits in the centre of row 6, The Time of Penance. One arrow ends here: the arrow of Apt religion from square 28, which carries the player from row 4 directly to the sixth row. A player can also arrive by an ordinary throw from the squares below. Square 50 itself has no arrow and no snake, so the next throw moves the player on by count.
50.gita: Gita 17.14 describes austerity of body, speech and mind, and calls it sattvic only when practised with faith and without craving for reward, never as self-torment. Arjuna's penance, and his humbling meeting with Shiva disguised as the Kirata hunter, shows tapas that ends not in pride but in grace received.
questions: Which discipline would set me free?
Is my effort an offering, or a way of proving something?
Where has my discipline become harsh with me or with others?

51.intro: Square 51 in Leela is Earth, prithvi in Sanskrit. Johari calls it the Great Mother and the stage on which the whole game is played. It is also where the snake from square 72, Inertia, brings back a player who passed the goal. Earth is not a punishment but a fresh starting point, three squares below Spiritual devotion.
meaning: Johari describes Earth as the Great Mother, the ground that holds every being and the stage on which Leela, the divine play, unfolds. Players carried to the top of the board by arrows return here to work their way up again. The square is less about falling than about being received.

The Sanskrit prithvi names the earth element and the goddess of the earth, the broad and patient one. Earth is also the element of the first chakra, at the base of the spine. Finding it again in row 6 says something important: even near the top of the board, the player is still standing on solid ground and still has a body, a place and work to do.

Square 51 belongs to row 6, The Time of Penance, and the Ajna chakra. Johari points out that from here Spiritual devotion at 54 is only one throw of the die away. A player who returns to Earth is therefore close to the one arrow that leads straight to the goal.
What square 51 teaches is the dignity of beginning again. A return is not a failure. It is the chance to act once more, with what the earlier flight has shown you.
51.board: Square 51 sits in row 6, The Time of Penance. One snake ends here: the snake of Inertia on square 72, which brings back a player who went past 68 into the top row. A player can also arrive by an ordinary throw from below. Earth has no arrow or snake of its own, and the arrow of Spiritual devotion at 54 is just three squares ahead.
51.gita: Gita 9.21 says that when merit is spent, those who tasted heaven return to the mortal world; this square treats that return as a place to act again. Yayati, who fell from heaven after boasting of his own merit, shows how pride ends the flight and how the earth receives the one who falls.
questions: Where will my new ascent begin?
What did my last high point teach me that I can use now?
What ground under my feet am I grateful for?

52.intro: Square 52 in Leela is the Plane of violence, himsa-loka. It is the danger of the sixth chakra: zeal and force used in the name of an idea, even a spiritual one. A snake waits here. It draws the player down to square 35, Purgatory, in the fourth row, where Johari says the harm done must be atoned for.
meaning: Johari places violence high on the board, in the row of penance, and the placement is deliberate. This is not the crude aggression of the lower chakras. It is the violence of conviction: the zealot who knows that no one truly dies and therefore feels entitled to wage holy wars. Insight without humility becomes a licence.

The Sanskrit himsa means harm, injury, the will to hurt. Its opposite, ahimsa, is one of the first principles of yoga. That this square sits only two places after the Plane of austerity is a lesson in itself: the heat of discipline, turned outward or turned harshly inward, can become harm.

Square 52 belongs to row 6, The Time of Penance, and the Ajna chakra. The third eye gives clarity, and clarity can harden into certainty. When a player forces themselves or others to fit an idea, they lose the very discernment this row is meant to build.

The snake does not punish for its own sake. It shows where force leads: to Purgatory, the square of atonement, where one faces the effects of what was done and begins to repair. Repair begins with seeing clearly, without excuses and without self-hatred, what one's certainty has cost others.
52.board: Square 52 sits in row 6, The Time of Penance, and is reached by an ordinary throw, since no arrow or snake ends here. It is the head of a snake. A player who lands on 52 slides down to square 35, Purgatory, falling from row 6 to row 4, where the climb continues after atonement.
52.gita: Gita 2.19 teaches that the Self neither kills nor is killed, but that is no excuse for violence: action without ego is nothing like cruelty in the name of an idea. Ashvatthama's night raid on the sleeping Pandava camp is the epic's darkest picture of that confusion.
questions: Where am I forcing myself or others?
Which belief of mine has become a reason to stop listening?
What would repair look like where I have caused harm?

53.intro: Square 53 in Leela is the Liquid plane, jala-loka, the plane of water. Johari describes it as cooling waters that quench the heat of austerity and violence, the two fiery squares just before it in row 6. It teaches fluidity: the ability to move around obstacles, adapt and stay calm instead of forcing your way through.
meaning: Johari's meaning is short and vivid: the Liquid plane brings cooling waters that quench the heat of austerity and violence. After the inner fire of tapas at 50 and the scorching zeal of 52, the player meets water. The square restores balance.

The Sanskrit jala means water, and loka means plane or world. Water is the element of the second chakra, linked to feeling and flow. Meeting it again in row 6 suggests that refined discernment still needs softness. Water does not fight a stone; it goes around it, and over time shapes it.

Square 53 belongs to row 6, The Time of Penance, and the Ajna chakra. Johari adds a striking line here: the game starts in the sixth chakra. Below it the player is largely moved by circumstance; from this row on, the inner work becomes conscious and chosen. Fluidity is what makes that work sustainable.

What the square teaches is a different kind of strength. Calm, adaptable and receptive, the player can hold strong experiences without being swept away. Next to it waits square 54, Spiritual devotion, as if the water were flowing on toward the ocean. Rest in this square before taking the next step, and notice what softens when you stop resisting.
53.board: Square 53 sits in row 6, The Time of Penance, after the Plane of violence at 52 and before Spiritual devotion at 54. No arrow or snake ends here, so a player arrives by an ordinary throw. It is a plain square with nothing to climb or fall, and the arrow of devotion is only one square ahead.
53.gita: Gita 2.70 compares the sage to the ocean, which takes in all rivers and stays still: full and calm, like deep water. When Arjuna shoots an arrow into the earth so that a spring rises for the dying Bhishma, water becomes an act of care in the middle of war.
questions: Where do I need to flow instead of push?
What obstacle could I go around rather than break?
What cools me down when I am burning with effort or anger?

54.intro: Square 54 in Leela is Spiritual devotion, bhakti-loka. It holds the most important arrow on the board: the only one that leads straight to the goal, square 68, Cosmic Consciousness. Johari calls it the arrow that takes the drop to the ocean. In this game of self-knowledge, love and surrender reach further than knowledge alone.
meaning: Johari describes Spiritual devotion as love of the Deity, and its arrow as the one that takes the drop to the ocean. The individual self, a drop that has wandered across the board, returns to its source. He calls it the only direct path to liberation in the game.

The Sanskrit bhakti comes from a root meaning to share in, to belong to. Devotion is not an emotion to be produced but a turning of the whole heart toward what one serves. The board makes a clear point here: the arrow of Right knowledge at 45 stops one square short of the goal, at 67, while devotion lands on 68 itself.

Square 54 is the last square of row 6, The Time of Penance, and belongs to the Ajna chakra. After the effort of austerity, the danger of violence and the cooling of water, the row ends in surrender. Johari also notes that from Earth, at 51, this square is only one throw away.

What it teaches is that the deepest movement is not taken but given. Devotion does not require perfection, only wholeheartedness. It is the quality the Gita places at the very end of its teaching. On this square, devotion is a direction of the heart.
54.board: Square 54 sits at the end of row 6, The Time of Penance, three squares above Earth at 51. No arrow or snake ends here, so a player arrives by an ordinary throw. It is the base of an arrow: a player who lands on 54 climbs at once to square 68, Cosmic Consciousness, rising from row 6 to row 8. Landing exactly on 68 ends the game.
54.gita: In Gita 18.65 Krishna gives his final promise: fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, and you will come to Me. When Draupadi, humiliated in the assembly hall, stops defending herself and calls on Krishna with her whole being, she is held; that is the surrender this square describes.
questions: What do I want to serve with my whole heart?
What would I offer if I did not need anything back?
Where am I still holding on when I could let myself be held?

55.intro: Square 55 in Leela is Egotism, ahamkara, the first square of row 7 and the crown chakra. It is the separate self that resists the flow of life, and Johari says anger is the inevitable result. A long snake waits here: it drops the player from the seventh row all the way down to square 3, Anger.
meaning: Johari describes egotism as ahamkara cut off from the whole: the self identifying completely with the moving symbol on the board. In his words, if ahamkara fights the flow of sudharma, one's own right way, anger is the inevitable result. The rules put it more briefly: egotism leads to anger.

The Sanskrit ahamkara means the I-maker, the function that says this is mine, I did this. On its own it is a useful faculty. It becomes egotism when it forgets that it is part of something larger. Johari also defines it, in his framing of the board, as becoming elated with the arrow's rise and depressed with the serpent's bite.

Square 55 opens row 7, The Plane of Reality, and belongs to the Sahasrara chakra at the crown. This is the plane of truth, on the verge of liberation, and also the most dangerous row: three snakes and no arrows. Egotism is the first of them, waiting precisely where the player feels most advanced.

What it teaches is subtle. The risk near the top is not a lack of insight but ownership of it. Watching one's own movement without taking every rise and fall personally is the way through. Anger, when it comes, can then be read as a signal.
55.board: Square 55 is the first square of row 7, The Plane of Reality, reached by an ordinary throw from the end of row 6, since no arrow or snake ends here. It is the head of a snake. A player who lands on 55 slides down to square 3, Anger, falling from row 7 to row 1, one of the longest falls in the game.
55.gita: Gita 3.27 says that one deluded by ego thinks 'I am the doer', though the gunas of nature do the acting. Nahusha, raised to the throne of Indra and then fallen through his arrogance, is the epic's image of a high position lost to the sense of being its only author.
questions: What in me needs to be right?
Which recent success am I taking too personally?
Where does my anger show me that my ego feels threatened?

56.intro: Square 56 in Leela is the Plane of primal vibrations, named Omkar after Om, the sacred syllable. Johari describes it as the cosmic sound of creation and the basis of all knowledge and art. It sits in row 7, the crown chakra, and invites the player to listen for what vibrates beneath words and forms.
meaning: Johari's meaning is concise: Omkar is Om, the cosmic sound, the basis of all knowledge and art. In Indian thought the universe begins as vibration before it becomes form. Language, music, mathematics and every craft grow from that first sound.

The Sanskrit Omkar, or Omkara, means the form or making of Om. The syllable is chanted at the start and end of prayers and studies, and is often heard as three sounds, a, u and m, followed by silence. To land here is to touch the root from which every expression in the game comes.

Square 56 belongs to row 7, The Plane of Reality, and the Sahasrara chakra at the crown. This row is the plane of truth, close to liberation, and the elements reappear here in their subtlest forms: primal sound at 56, air at 57, light at 58. After Egotism at 55, the player meets something that cannot be owned, only heard.

What the square teaches is attention through listening. Before thinking or doing, there is a quality, a tone, in each person and moment. Hearing your own is a form of self-knowledge. On this square, the invitation is to be quiet long enough to hear it, and to let what you make grow from there.
56.board: Square 56 sits in row 7, The Plane of Reality, right after Egotism at 55. No arrow or snake leads here, so a player arrives by an ordinary throw. It is a plain square: nothing lifts or drops the player, who moves on by count with the next throw. Two snakes still lie ahead in this row, at 61 and 63.
56.gita: In Gita 8.13 the yogi who repeats Om while remembering the Highest reaches the supreme goal, and Krishna names himself the syllable Om in the Vedas. Vyasa dictating the Mahabharata to Ganesha, who writes without pause, shows the primal sound becoming knowledge and art.
questions: What is the sound of my soul?
When did I last listen to silence long enough to hear something?
Which of my creative expressions feels closest to its source?

57.intro: Square 57 in Leela is the Gaseous plane, vayu-loka, the plane of air. Johari describes it as the essence of air: weightlessness, formlessness and true freedom of action. It sits in row 7, the crown chakra, where the elements return in their subtlest form, and asks what it would take for a player to act without heaviness.
meaning: For Johari the Gaseous plane is the essence of air: weightless, formless and free. Air moves everywhere and is held by nothing. On this square the player tastes action that is not weighed down by fear, habit or the need for a particular result.

The Sanskrit vayu means wind or air, and also the god of the wind; loka means plane or world. Air is the element of the heart chakra, linked to movement and breath. Meeting it again near the crown, it is no longer feeling or longing but pure mobility, the ability to go where one is needed.

Square 57 belongs to row 7, The Plane of Reality, and the Sahasrara chakra. With 56 primal sound and 58 light, it forms a run of subtle elements in the plane of truth. Yet freedom can also scatter: the mind, too, is as restless as the wind. Real freedom of action keeps a still centre.

What the square teaches is lightness with direction. Letting go of what weighs you down is half of freedom. The other half is knowing what you are free for. On this square, the player can ask which habits and fears still keep them on the ground, and which direction their freedom wants to take.
57.board: Square 57 sits in row 7, The Plane of Reality, between Primal vibrations at 56 and Radiation at 58. No arrow or snake ends here, so a player arrives by an ordinary throw. It is a plain square with no climb and no fall. The player moves on by count, toward a part of the row where snakes wait at 61 and 63.
57.gita: Gita 9.6 says that as the mighty wind moves everywhere yet rests in space, all beings rest in the Highest; freedom of movement needs that resting place. When Bhima meets Hanuman, his elder brother through the wind god Vayu, and cannot lift the old monkey's tail, strength learns humility.
questions: What would make me freer?
What weight am I carrying that is no longer mine to carry?
Where in my life is there movement, and where is there stillness inside it?

58.intro: Square 58 in Leela is the Plane of radiation, teja-loka, the plane of light. Here, Johari says, the player begins to radiate. It sits in row 7, the crown chakra, and is a square no arrow reaches directly: a player can only arrive by moving step by step. Its light is not borrowed but grown from within.
meaning: Johari calls it the plane of light, taijas, where the player radiates. Up to this point light has been something to seek. On square 58 it becomes something the player gives off, simply by being who they have become.

The Sanskrit teja means fire, brilliance, radiance; it is also the name of the fire element in its subtle form. Fire belongs to the third chakra, the seat of will and digestion. In row 7 it is no longer the fire of ambition but a steady glow. Johari stresses that this plane is not directly attainable by any arrow: there is no shortcut to it.

Square 58 belongs to row 7, The Plane of Reality, and the Sahasrara chakra. It completes a sequence of subtle elements: primal sound at 56, air at 57, light at 58. Next to it lies 59, the Plane of reality, the last of the seven lokas.

What it teaches is that real radiance is a by-product, not a goal. Those who try to shine usually cast shadows. Those who do their work and stay open let the light through. On this square, the question is not how to become brighter, but what in you still stands in the way of a light that is already there.
58.board: Square 58 sits in row 7, The Plane of Reality, between the Gaseous plane at 57 and the Plane of reality at 59. No arrow or snake ends here; Johari notes it cannot be reached directly by any arrow, only by an ordinary throw. It is a plain square, so the player moves on by count with the next throw.
58.gita: In Gita 15.12 Krishna says the radiance of sun, moon and fire is his, so every spark of beauty, including yours, is part of that light. Karna, son of the sun, born with radiant armour and earrings, gives them away when asked, and his light shows most in that generosity.
questions: How do I shine for others?
When do I try to shine, and when do I simply let light through?
Who has been a light for me, and what did they do?

59.intro: Square 59 in Leela is the Plane of reality, satya-loka, the seventh and last loka on the board's central spine. It is the plane of truth, on the threshold of liberation. Yet Johari warns that no more arrows lie ahead of the player here, only snakes. Square 59 asks what is truly real, and whether you will go all the way.
meaning: Johari describes satya-loka as the seventh and last loka, on the verge of liberation, yet with three snakes still in its row. In his words, there are no more arrows ahead of him. From now on the player cannot be lifted; they can only walk on, or fall.

The Sanskrit satya means truth, and also that which truly is. Satya-loka is, in Indian cosmology, the highest of the seven worlds, the world of Brahma. Reaching it is a great thing, but even this world, the tradition says, is not the end. Truth is a threshold to cross, not a place to settle.

Square 59 is the central plane of row 7, The Plane of Reality, and of the Sahasrara chakra at the crown. It stands on the spine of the board, directly below 68 Vaikuntha, Cosmic Consciousness. Around it wait the three snakes of the row: Egotism at 55, Negative intellect at 61, Darkness at 63.

What it teaches is honesty at the highest level. Half-truths, small evasions and spiritual pride are exactly what the snakes of this row feed on. The way forward is simple truthfulness, kept to the end. On this square, truth becomes practical: a word kept, a fact admitted, a pretence dropped.
59.board: Square 59 sits in the centre of row 7, The Plane of Reality, directly below the goal. No arrow or snake ends here, so a player arrives by an ordinary throw. It is a plain square. From here no arrows remain on the way ahead, and the snakes of Negative intellect at 61 and Darkness at 63 lie within reach of the next throw.
59.gita: Gita 8.16 says that even the world of Brahma is subject to return, and only one who reaches the Highest is not born again: do not stop at the threshold. Yudhishthira's half-truth at Drona's death, a single shading of the truth by the most truthful of the brothers, shows how close to the top a fall can begin.
questions: What is truly real for me?
Where am I telling myself a half-truth?
What would it mean to go all the way rather than stop at the threshold?

60.intro: Square 60 in Leela is Positive intellect, subuddhi: clear, non-dual understanding. Johari calls it, together with dharma, one of the two most potent tools in the game. It is reached by the arrow from square 22, the Plane of dharma, which lifts the player from row 3 to row 7, showing that right understanding grows from right action.
meaning: Johari describes Positive intellect as non-dual right understanding. It sees things whole, without splitting the world into me and not me, for and against. Johari ranks it with dharma as "two of the most potent tools in the game": one is right action, the other right understanding.

The Sanskrit subuddhi joins su, good or right, with buddhi, the intellect that discerns and decides. Buddhi is the faculty that can reflect the Self clearly, as still water reflects the moon. Johari says positive intellect is achieved by following the path of dharma, the source of the arrow that ends here. Clarity, in this game, is the fruit of how one has lived.

Square 60 belongs to row 7, The Plane of Reality, and the Sahasrara chakra at the crown. It has a twin right beside it: 61, Negative intellect, a snake that drops the doubting mind to Nullity. The two squares sit side by side, as if to show that the same faculty can lift or ruin.

What it teaches is decisiveness rooted in clarity. A mind gathered to one point sees the next step and takes it, without endless second thoughts. On this square, the player can trust a clear mind, and keep it clear by acting on what it already sees.
60.board: Square 60 sits in row 7, The Plane of Reality. One arrow ends here: the arrow of the Plane of dharma from square 22, which lifts the player from row 3 straight to row 7. A player can also arrive by an ordinary throw. Square 60 has no arrow or snake of its own, but the snake of Negative intellect waits on the very next square, 61.
60.gita: Gita 2.41 says the resolute mind is one-pointed while the irresolute branches endlessly, so gather attention to a single point and the way becomes clear. In the Yaksha's questions, Yudhishthira answers riddle after riddle at the lake with a calm, clear mind, and his brothers' lives are given back.
questions: What decision does my clear mind suggest?
Where am I branching into endless options instead of choosing?
Which of my past right actions is now giving me clarity?

61.intro: Square 61 in Leela is Negative intellect, durbuddhi in Sanskrit. It sits in the seventh row, the Plane of Reality, at the level of the crown chakra, and its head is a snake. In Harish Johari's reading, a mind that doubts the divine presence turns its own sharpness against itself and falls to square 13, Nullity.
meaning: Johari describes negative intellect as the state in which the player, very close to the goal, begins to doubt the divine presence. The doubt is not a lack of intelligence. It is intelligence turned upside down, a mind that reasons well yet takes its own cleverness as the last word and starts to treat what is false as true.

The Sanskrit name says it plainly. Buddhi is the discerning intellect, the faculty that sees and decides; the prefix dur marks something gone wrong or ill directed. Durbuddhi is the exact counterpart of square 60, subuddhi, Positive intellect, which stands right next to it. The board places the two side by side on purpose: the same faculty, two directions.

Its place makes the lesson sharper. Row 7 belongs to Sahasrara, the crown, and to satya-loka, the plane of reality at square 59. A player here has come a long way, and Johari notes that this row holds three snakes and no arrows. Square 61 teaches that refinement of thought does not protect anyone by itself. Without humility and trust, a brilliant mind can still undo the whole climb in one movement, and the fall is not into ordinary passion but into emptiness.
61.board: There are no arrows or snakes that end on square 61, so a player only reaches it by count from squares 56 to 60 in the same row, often just after Positive intellect at 60. Landing here means meeting the head of a snake: the symbol drops at once from the seventh row to square 13, Nullity, in the second row. From there Johari says only the arrows of Mercy (17) or Charity (20) can lift the player quickly again.
61.gita: The verse linked to square 61 is Gita 18.32: tamasic understanding takes adharma for dharma and sees everything upside down. Duryodhana rejecting Krishna's peace offer shows this inverted intellect at work, a clever mind refusing the one voice that could have saved it.
questions: Which thoughts am I letting run me?
Where am I using reasoning to avoid trusting something I already sense is true?
If my view of this situation were upside down, what would the right way up look like?

62.intro: Square 62 in Leela is Happiness, sukh in Sanskrit, in the seventh row at the level of the crown chakra. Johari describes it as a balance of body chemistry and psyche felt very near the goal. It is a gift, often reached by the arrow of Conscience, but it carries a warning: contentment that turns into complacency calls darkness in.
meaning: In Johari's commentary, happiness is the natural result of a body and psyche in balance. Nothing is pulling the player in two directions; desire has quietened and the inner chemistry is at ease. This is not pleasure from an object but a settled state, and it appears high on the board, close to Cosmic Consciousness.

The Sanskrit word sukh is the everyday word for ease and well being, the opposite of dukh, suffering. Its root image is a wheel turning smoothly on its axle. Here it describes a player whose inner wheel runs true, which is why it can be reached directly from square 46, Conscience: when the inner voice is followed, life stops grinding.

The danger lies in the very next square. Square 63 is tamas, darkness, the head of the longest snake in the game. Johari reads this placement as a teaching: happiness that becomes satisfied with itself slows into inertia, and inertia mistakes itself for completion. Row 7, the Plane of Reality, is a row with three snakes and no arrows, so square 62 asks the player to enjoy the ease without resting on it. Happiness here is a place to breathe, not a place to stop.
62.board: Square 62 is reached by count or by the arrow from square 46, Conscience, which lifts the player from the sixth row straight into the seventh. It is a plain square with no snake and no arrow leaving it, so the symbol stays and waits for the next throw. That throw matters: a one lands on 63, Darkness, and the long snake down to square 2, Illusion.
62.gita: Gita 18.37 is the verse for square 62: sattvic happiness is like poison at first and nectar at the end, while rajasic happiness is the reverse. The path from the Rajasuya to the dice game shows a joy that faded because it was taken for granted.
questions: What makes me happy with no conditions attached?
Where has my contentment quietly become an excuse to stop moving?
Which joy in my life grows over time, and which one fades as soon as I have it?

63.intro: Square 63 in Leela is Darkness, tamas in Sanskrit, the last square of the seventh row at the level of the crown chakra. It is the head of the longest snake in the game. Johari describes it as inaction mistaken for completion: a player who believes the work is done slides all the way back to square 2, Illusion.
meaning: Johari calls this the longest snake in the game, one that draws the player back into illusion without fail. Its cause is subtle. The player has reached the top of the crown chakra, has tasted happiness at 62, and now settles. Nothing dramatic happens; there is no anger or greed. There is only a stopping, a heaviness that presents itself as having arrived.

Tamas is one of the three gunas, the qualities of nature, alongside sattva and rajas. It is the quality of weight, dullness, sleep and darkness. In everyday life it is necessary, since rest and stability depend on it, but when it governs the mind it covers clarity like a cloud. The same guna returns at the very end of the board as square 72, Tamoguna.

The placement at the end of row 7 makes the teaching memorable. Row 7, the Plane of Reality, holds satya-loka at 59, yet Johari notes it contains three snakes and no arrows. Square 63 shows that the greatest risk near the summit is not a vice but inertia. The fall to square 2, Illusion, means starting again almost from the beginning, which is why the square asks for one more step instead of rest.
63.board: No arrow or snake ends on square 63, so a player reaches it only by count, often from square 62, Happiness, or from earlier squares of row 7. Landing here triggers the longest snake on the board: the symbol falls from the seventh row to square 2, Illusion, in the first row, close to where the journey began at 6, Delusion. The climb then starts again through the first chakra.
63.gita: Square 63 is linked to Gita 14.8: tamas is born of ignorance and deludes all embodied beings. Ashvatthama's night raid shows darkness acting in the dark, and the verse's lesson is that even a small act beats inaction.
questions: Where have I frozen?
What am I calling finished that is in fact only abandoned?
What is one small step I could take today towards the light?

64.intro: Square 64 in Leela is the Phenomenal plane, prakriti-loka in Sanskrit. It opens the eighth and top row, The Gods Themselves, which lies beyond the chakras. Johari describes it as prakriti, nature both divine and manifest, seen from within: the player now apprehends the gunas and the elements in their essence rather than through their surface forms.
meaning: After seven rows that map the chakras of the body, square 64 marks a change of view. In Johari's commentary the player here apprehends the three gunas and the elements in their essence. Nature is no longer a set of objects to want or avoid; it is seen as one living process, divine and manifest at once.

Prakriti is the Sanskrit term for primordial nature, the source of everything that takes form, and loka means plane or world. In Indian thought prakriti is woven from the three gunas, sattva, rajas and tamas, and unfolds as the elements together with mind, intellect and ego. Johari reads the eight rows of the board in the same way: eight stands for prakriti, nine for the Absolute.

Its position is telling. Square 64 sits at the top right corner, the start of a row that holds the triad of Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma at 67, 68 and 69 and closes with the three gunas at 70, 71 and 72. Before reaching the gods, the player sees the stage on which the whole game has been played. The lesson is clear seeing: what looked solid is play, and behind the play stands a living principle.
64.board: No arrow or snake ends on square 64, so a player arrives only by count, moving up from the last squares of row 7, the Plane of Reality. It is a plain square with nothing to climb or fall. From here a throw of exactly four lands on 68, Cosmic Consciousness, and ends the game, while a five or six carries the symbol past the goal into 69 or 70.
64.gita: Gita 7.4 belongs to square 64: Krishna's nature is eightfold, earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego. The episode of Krishna's cosmic form in the Kaurava court shows the whole of manifest nature revealed as one living play.
questions: What do I see when I look beneath the form?
Which part of my situation is simply nature at play, and which part is mine to act on?
Where can I sense the same living principle in people I usually see only from outside?

65.intro: Square 65 in Leela is the Plane of inner space, uranta-loka in Sanskrit, in the eighth row beyond the chakras. Johari describes it as the place where the feeling self ends. Duality falls away, and the player experiences an inner space without limits, three squares from Cosmic Consciousness at 68.
meaning: Johari's key phrase for this square is the point where the feeling self ends. Up to here the player has known the world through sensation and emotion, always as someone who feels something. On square 65 that subject quietens. With no one standing apart to feel, the division between inside and outside stops operating, and duality dissolves. What remains is presence, quiet and wide.

The name uranta-loka belongs with Johari's image of an ending: a boundary where one way of being stops and a wider one begins. What opens beyond that boundary is space: not emptiness in the sense of loss, as at square 13, Nullity, but spaciousness, a room inside large enough to hold every thought without being shaped by any of them.

In the top row, The Gods Themselves, square 65 follows the Phenomenal plane at 64. First nature is seen clearly; then the seer finds the space in which seeing happens. It prepares the player for bliss at 66 and for the goal at 68. The square teaches that the self is more than its content: thoughts, moods and roles move through a space they never fill. Nothing has to be pushed away for this space to appear; it is noticed in the gap between two thoughts.
65.board: No arrow or snake leads to square 65, so a player arrives only by count, from row 7 or from square 64. It is a plain square with no arrow and no snake. From here a throw of exactly three reaches 68, Cosmic Consciousness, and ends the game. A four, five or six carries the symbol past the goal into 69, 70 or 71, where the top row's long detour begins.
65.gita: Gita 13.32 is the verse for square 65: as all-pervading space is never stained, being so subtle, the Self in the body stays pure. Markandeya inside the divine child, discovering whole worlds within, gives the image of an inner space larger than the one who holds it.
questions: What is in me besides my thoughts?
When I stop feeling for a moment, what is left?
Which inner space could hold this problem without being shaped by it?

66.intro: Square 66 in Leela is the Plane of bliss, ananda-loka in Sanskrit, in the eighth row beyond the chakras. Johari links it to the anandamaya kosha, the innermost sheath of bliss. Only one feeling remains here, the feeling of bliss. The arrow of True awareness from square 37 lands on it, two squares from Cosmic Consciousness.
meaning: Johari describes the Plane of bliss as the state in which only one feeling remains: bliss. Fear, desire, pride and sorrow have fallen away one by one over the course of the board. What is left is not excitement or pleasure but a quiet, steady joy that needs nothing to sustain it.

Ananda is the Sanskrit word for bliss, and in the Indian picture of the person it is the subtlest of five sheaths, the koshas, that wrap the Self: body, breath, mind, intellect and finally bliss. The anandamaya kosha is the closest layer to the Self itself, which is why this square sits so near the goal. It differs from square 62, Happiness, which depends on a balance of body and psyche; ananda does not depend on conditions at all.

The square is reached most directly by the arrow from 37, True awareness, gyana. Johari's message is that real knowledge does not end in more concepts but in joy. Placed in the row of the gods, after inner space at 65 and before Shiva's plane at 67, bliss is one of the last veils. The teaching is gentle: welcome it fully, and do not cling to it, since even bliss is a step and not the goal.
66.board: A player reaches square 66 by count or by the arrow from square 37, True awareness (gyana), which rises from the fifth row straight into the eighth. Square 66 itself is plain, with no snake and no arrow. From here an exact two lands on 68, Cosmic Consciousness, and ends the game. Throws of three to six carry the symbol past the goal into 69 to 72.
66.gita: Gita 6.21 is linked to square 66: there is a happiness beyond the senses, grasped by the intellect, and having found it the yogi does not waver. Sanjaya's divine vision, seeing far beyond what his eyes could reach, mirrors this joy that the senses do not supply.
questions: What brings me quiet joy?
Which joy in me needs nothing outside to keep it alive?
Can I let this moment of joy be complete without trying to hold on to it?

67.intro: Square 67 in Leela is the Plane of cosmic good, Rudra-loka in Sanskrit, the abode of Shiva in the eighth row beyond the chakras. Johari describes the good here as cosmic: its essence is truth and its form is beauty. The arrow of Right knowledge from square 45 lands on it, leaving the player one square from Cosmic Consciousness.
meaning: In Johari's commentary the right, at this height, becomes cosmic good. It is no longer a rule to follow or a preference of one group; it is the order of the whole. Its essence is truth and its form is beauty, so that what is good, what is true and what is beautiful are seen to be one thing from three sides.

Rudra is an ancient name of Shiva, and Rudra-loka means the world of Rudra. Shiva is the transformer, the one who dissolves what has served its time so that something truer can appear. Square 67 forms, with 68 Vaikuntha-loka of Vishnu and 69 Brahma-loka of Brahma, the divine triad that Johari places side by side in the middle of the top row.

The square has a particular lesson about knowledge. The arrow of Right knowledge from 45 brings the player here, and Johari observes that the player is now one square away from the goal. Yet knowledge stops short: only the arrow of Devotion from 54 lands on 68 itself. Square 67 honours what clear understanding achieves and shows its limit. The last step asks for something beyond knowing, a surrender of the one who knows.
67.board: A player reaches square 67 by count or by the arrow from square 45, Right knowledge, which rises from the fifth row to the eighth. Square 67 is plain, with no snake and no arrow leaving it. From here only a one reaches 68, Cosmic Consciousness. A two to five carries the symbol past the goal to 69, 70, 71 or 72. A six brings another throw, and together they carry the symbol beyond 72: on Leela Atlas it goes up to 72, down the snake to 51, Earth, and plays the rest of the throw from there.
67.gita: Gita 10.23 is the verse for square 67: among the Rudras Krishna is Shankara. The episode of Arjuna, the Kirata and the Pashupata weapon shows Shiva granting the highest gift only after Arjuna has been tested in both humility and strength.
questions: What would be good for everyone?
Where do the true, the good and the beautiful already meet in my life?
What do I understand clearly but have not yet surrendered to?

68.intro: Square 68 in Leela is Cosmic Consciousness, Vaikuntha-loka in Sanskrit, the abode of Vishnu at the top centre of the board. It is both the start and the goal. Every symbol waits here unborn until a six is thrown, and the game ends when a player lands on it exactly, by count or by the arrow of Spiritual devotion from square 54.
meaning: For Johari, square 68 is liberation. When the player lands here, the ring or personal object that stood for him in the game goes back to his finger, and the game stops. The symbol that wandered through seventy two states of being returns to the one who placed it on the board. Nothing more needs to be gained.

Vaikuntha is the name of Vishnu's realm, often read as the place without hindrance or limitation. It is the eighth and last of the planes in the central column of the board, the spine that runs from 5 Bhu-loka through 59 Satya-loka. Together with Shiva's world at 67 and Brahma's world at 69, it forms the divine triad of the top row, with Vishnu, the preserver, at its heart.

The square closes a circle. Every player begins on 68, unborn, and needs a six to enter the game at Genesis and Delusion. The whole board is the journey back. Johari names three paths after arrival: to play again, to remain beyond the game, or to return to earth as a twice born bodhisattva to help others. In practice the player also states what has become clear about the question or intention brought to the game.
68.board: Before play, every symbol sits on square 68 and waits for a six. To end the game a player must land on 68 exactly: by count, for example a two from 66, or by the arrow from square 54, Spiritual devotion, the only direct route to the goal. A throw that overshoots carries the symbol into 69 to 72, where the snake at 72 returns it to Earth.
68.gita: Gita 8.21 is the verse for square 68: there is a supreme abode from which no one returns, lit by neither sun, moon nor fire. Yudhishthira refusing to enter heaven without the faithful dog shows the loyalty and surrender with which that abode is reached.
questions: What has become clear about my question?
What did I let go of on the way that I no longer need to carry?
Having arrived, would I choose to play again, to rest, or to return and help?

69.intro: Square 69 in Leela is the Absolute plane, Brahma-loka in Sanskrit, the world of Brahma in the eighth row, just past the goal. It is reached by the arrow of Mercy from square 17 or by overshooting 68. Johari explains that Brahma decrees form but cannot liberate the player, so play must go on.
meaning: Johari's description is precise: Brahma is the creator, the one who decrees form, and his world is very high. Yet he cannot liberate the player. On square 69 form still remains, and with form the remains of karma. The player has reached a summit that is not the goal, and tamoguna at 72 will eventually return him to earth. It resembles a great success that still leaves unfinished business behind.

Brahma-loka means the world of Brahma, the highest of the created worlds in Indian cosmology. The name Absolute plane can mislead: it is the peak of manifestation, not the escape from it.
