Square 69 completes the divine triad of the top row with Shiva at 67 and Vishnu at 68. Of the three, only Vishnu's Vaikuntha is the end of the game.

The most striking route here is the arrow of Mercy from square 17, which Johari describes as lifting the player from the second chakra straight to the eighth. Compassion is so powerful that it carries a beginner past almost the whole board. But because past karma has not been worked through, the player is not free. Square 69 teaches that even the highest attainment is not liberation, and that it is wise not to cling to it.
69.board: A player reaches square 69 by the arrow from square 17, Mercy, or by a throw that overshoots 68 from below. Square 69 is plain, with no snake and no arrow. From here the way forward is only through the top row: a one or two moves to 70 or 71, a three reaches 72, whose snake returns the symbol to 51, Earth, and on Leela Atlas a larger throw goes up to 72, down to 51 and plays its rest from there.
69.gita: Square 69 is linked to Gita 8.16: the worlds up to Brahma's lead back to return. Yayati's fall from heaven, after his merit ran out, shows how a high world reached by good deeds is still a stay and not a home.
questions: What am I still missing to complete this?
Which achievement am I treating as the end when it is only a high point?
What karma from earlier have I skipped over rather than worked through?

70.intro: Square 70 in Leela is True nature, satoguna in Sanskrit, the guna of sattva, in the top row beyond the chakras. It is reached by passing the goal at 68. Johari explains that truth bound to the karma die appears here through the three gunas, but the ring is still there: the player has not been freed and must return to earth.
meaning: Johari places the three gunas at the very end of the board, and sattva comes first. Here truth, still bound to the karma die, shows itself through the qualities of nature. The player's state is clear, light and harmonious. Yet Johari's point is simple and firm: the ring that stands for the player is still on the board. A pure state is not the same as liberation.

Satoguna, or sattvaguna, is the guna of sattva: purity, light, balance and knowledge. Of the three qualities it is the closest to truth, which is why Johari calls it true nature. Rajas, activity, follows at 71, and tamas, inertia, at 72. Together the three describe all of prakriti, and they close the board as the last thing a player passes through before falling back to earth.

The lesson of square 70 is subtle. It is easy to see greed or anger as obstacles; it is harder to see goodness as one. Sattva binds through attachment to happiness and to knowledge, to the satisfaction of being right or being good. A player who has overshot the goal discovers that purity can also become a place to sit. The square invites holding even virtue lightly.
70.board: No arrow or snake leads to square 70; a player arrives only by overshooting 68, from 64 with a six or from 65, 66, 67 or 69 by count. It is a plain square with no arrow and no snake. From here a two reaches 72, a one moves to 71, and on Leela Atlas a larger throw goes up to 72, down its snake to 51 and carries on from there. The way back to the goal runs through 72 and Earth.
70.gita: Gita 14.6 is the verse for square 70: sattva is pure and illuminating, yet it too binds, through attachment to happiness and knowledge. Vidura, the counsellor of dharma, wise and upright yet still bound to the court he served, embodies this luminous but binding quality.
questions: Where is my purity turning into attachment?
Which of my virtues do I hold on to because it makes me feel right?
What would it mean to be good without needing to be seen as good?

71.intro: Square 71 in Leela is Activity, rajoguna in Sanskrit, the guna of rajas, in the top row beyond the chakras. Johari describes it as karma and activity after failing to attain 68. The player has passed the goal and is still moving. Unless this energy is converted into sattva, Johari says, it becomes the cause of suffering.
meaning: In Johari's commentary rajoguna is what happens when a player misses Cosmic Consciousness and keeps going. Energy that could have come to rest turns into more activity and more karma. Action itself is not the problem; the board is full of virtuous actions. The problem is momentum without direction, action driven by the need to act. Most people know this moment: a target is missed, and instead of pausing they reach at once for the next task.

Rajas is the second of the three gunas: motion, passion, desire and drive. It is the force that gets things done and the force that cannot sit still. Between sattva at 70, clarity, and tamas at 72, inertia, rajas sits in the middle of the last three squares, just as in life restlessness often swings between brightness and collapse.

Johari's remedy is conversion. The same energy, refined, becomes sattva: action that is calm, offered and free of craving. Left as it is, rajoguna is the root of suffering, because it ties every act to a result that must be chased. Square 71 asks the player to notice the rush. It sits one square from the snake at 72, a reminder that hurried action, unexamined, leads straight back down. Sometimes the most precise act here is an honest pause.
71.board: No arrow or snake leads to square 71. A player arrives only after overshooting 68, by count from 65, 66, 67, 69 or 70. It is a plain square with no arrow and no snake. From here a one moves the symbol to 72, whose snake returns it to 51, Earth. On Leela Atlas a larger throw does the same and goes on from 51 with the rest of its count.
71.gita: Square 71 is linked to Gita 14.7: rajas is passion born of craving and attachment, and it binds through attachment to action. Arjuna's vow to slay Jayadratha before sunset, made in grief and anger, shows action driven by urgency rather than clarity.
questions: What am I rushing towards?
If I stopped for one day, what would I be afraid of missing?
Which of my actions could become calmer without becoming smaller?

72.intro: Square 72 in Leela is Inertia, tamoguna in Sanskrit, the last square of the board at its top left corner. It is the guna of tamas, and Johari describes it as a snake that bites the player and brings him back to earth. Every flight past the goal ends here, at square 51, Earth, from where the climb begins again.
meaning: For Johari, square 72 is the final teaching of the board. It comes in the form of a snake. Whoever has passed the goal, whether by overshooting 68 or by riding the arrow of Mercy to 69, eventually meets it. The bite does not punish; it returns. Inertia brings the player back to earth, where unfinished karma can be lived through.

Tamoguna is the guna of tamas, the quality of heaviness, darkness and sleep. It already appeared at square 63, Darkness, as the longest snake in the game. Here it closes the three gunas of the top row after sattva at 70 and rajas at 71. Together they show that every quality of nature, even the purest, keeps the player within the world until something beyond them is reached.

The snake lands on 51, Earth, which Johari describes as the Great Mother and the stage of the whole game. It is a soft landing compared with the falls into the first row, and it lies three squares below the arrow of Spiritual devotion at 54. The lesson is hopeful: even after missing the goal, the way home is near, and it passes through devotion. Returning does not cancel the journey; what was learned stays with the player.
72.board: No arrow or snake ends on square 72; a player arrives only from the top row, by an exact throw from 69, 70 or 71, or straight from 66 or 67 when the throw overshoots 68. On Leela Atlas a throw that would go beyond 72 also comes up to 72. Landing here triggers the snake: the symbol drops from the eighth row to square 51, Earth, in the sixth, and any rest of the throw is played from there. From Earth a three reaches 54 and the arrow to 68.
72.gita: Gita 14.8 is the verse for square 72: tamas binds through negligence, sloth and sleep, and those stuck in the lowest guna sink. The end of the Yadavas, a powerful clan undone by heedlessness after its greatest days, shows inertia striking even at the height of success.
questions: What keeps pulling me down, again and again?
Where in my life do I stop paying attention once things are going well?
What could I begin again today, with what I know now?
